title: Removing a forced 'Register' step at checkout: the "$300 million button"
summary: Jared Spool describes usability testing of an unnamed large retailer's checkout, where shoppers balked at a login/register form placed before payment. Replacing the Register button with a Continue button (registration optional) is reported to have lifted purchasing customers by 45% and added $300 million in the first year.
problem: Checkout began with a form asking shoppers to log in or register. The design team assumed this helped repeat buyers and that first-timers would not mind registering.
research: Usability tests in which participants who needed to buy products brought shopping lists and were given money to buy them on the site. The team then analyzed the retailer's customer database and password-request logs.
insight: First-time shoppers resented being pushed to register ('I'm not here to enter into a relationship. I just want to buy something'). Repeat shoppers often could not remember which email or password they had used. The database showed 45% of customers had multiple registrations, and about 160,000 password requests a day, 75% of which never ended in a purchase.
change: The Register button was removed and replaced with a Continue button plus a message saying an account was not needed to buy; shoppers could optionally create one during checkout.
outcome: Per Spool: the number of customers purchasing went up 45%, extra purchases brought in $15 million in the first month, and $300,000,000 in extra revenue in the first year.
attribution: Direct in the story: the design change came straight from usability-test observations and log analysis. But the only account is the consultant's own article.
caveats: Told by Jared Spool, whose firm (UIE) did the work, so it is an agency writing about its own client. The retailer is never named and the figures have never been independently verified. No control group or test method is described; the numbers are a before/after claim. Widely retold, sometimes with details drifting.

sources.title: The $300 Million Button

title: Intuit spots Quicken being used at work and builds QuickBooks
summary: Survey data showed many Quicken customers were running the personal-finance product in offices for bookkeeping. Scott Cook says Intuit talked to those users, learned they wanted Quicken's simplicity for business accounting, and launched QuickBooks as accounting software 'with no accounting in it'.
problem: Quicken was designed for household finances. Intuit had no small-business product and was not looking to build one.
research: Customer survey data, followed by conversations with the users who reported using Quicken at work. Intuit is also known for its 'Follow Me Home' practice of watching customers use software in their own setting, though the source for this case does not tie that method to it specifically.
insight: Many respondents were using Quicken in their bookkeeping jobs, not at home, because they liked its simple checkbook-style approach and found conventional accounting software too complex.
change: Intuit built and launched QuickBooks, positioned as the first accounting software with no accounting in it.
outcome: Cook says QuickBooks outsold the competition within two months of launch, and that QuickBooks today makes up half of Intuit's business.
attribution: The founder directly credits the surprising survey result and follow-up conversations with the decision to create the product. The commercial outcome is the founder's own account.
caveats: Founder storytelling in a university talk, recounted decades later; no data published. The source gives the launch year as 1991 (other sources say 1992). Commercial success also depended on many other factors. Counted as a pivot/new-product decision rather than a measured research effect.

sources.title: Savor surprises: A conversation with Intuit co-founder Scott Cook

title: Clayton Christensen's milkshake study: commuters 'hire' a shake for a boring drive
summary: A fast-food chain's demographic segmentation and 'ideal milkshake' feedback had failed to lift sales. Observing a restaurant for a day and interviewing customers showed about 40% of shakes were bought early in the morning by commuters who wanted something filling and slow to consume one-handed in the car. The recommendation was a thicker morning shake and a separate thinner shake for kids.
problem: The chain had asked people fitting the typical milkshake-buyer profile what an ideal shake would be and changed the product accordingly, but sales did not improve.
research: A researcher working with Christensen spent a full day in one restaurant recording who bought shakes, when, and whether they ate in or left. The next morning he interviewed customers leaving with shakes about what job they were 'hiring' the shake to do. The number of interviews is not given.
insight: Around 40% of shakes were bought first thing in the morning, to go, by people facing a long, dull commute. They wanted something to occupy one free hand, keep them full until mid-morning and not make a mess on work clothes; a thick shake through a thin straw beat bagels or doughnuts on all counts. Demographics did not explain the purchase; the situation did.
change: Christensen's team recommended a thicker, more interesting morning shake (e.g. with fruit chunks) to last the commute, and a separate thinner shake for children in the afternoon.
outcome: The source does not report whether the chain made the changes or whether sales rose. The case is cited as the origin story for the jobs-to-be-done approach to research.
attribution: The research clearly produced the recommendation, but there is no documented business outcome.
caveats: Classic teaching story told by Christensen in talks and books; the chain is never named in the original HBS write-up (it is often assumed to be McDonald's in retellings, which is not confirmed there). No sample sizes, dates or sales results are published. Include as a famous illustration of a research reframing, not as proof of impact.

title: Bank of America 'Keep the Change' grew from watching people round up
summary: IDEO and Bank of America's innovation team observed people in three US cities and noticed they routinely rounded up transactions for convenience, while many mothers struggled to save. The resulting service rounds debit card purchases up to the next dollar and moves the difference to savings. It reportedly attracted 2.5 million customers.
problem: Bank of America wanted to attract new account holders, particularly in a target audience of mothers.
research: Field observation by IDEO alongside members of Bank of America's innovation team in Atlanta, Baltimore and San Francisco (around 2004–2005). Sample size and session details are not published in the source.
insight: People in the target audience and beyond often rounded up their financial transactions for speed and convenience, and many mothers had trouble saving, whether for lack of money or willpower.
change: The bank launched 'Keep the Change', which rounds purchases on a Bank of America Visa debit card up to the nearest dollar and transfers the difference from checking to savings.
outcome: Core77 reports the program 'attracted 2.5 million customers', translating into more than 700,000 new checking accounts and one million new savings accounts.
attribution: The product concept is directly credited to the observed rounding behaviour. Account growth is reported, but the share caused by this program versus marketing and other factors is unknown.
caveats: Figures appear to come from IDEO/Bank of America material repeated in design press; no method for counting 'attracted' customers is given. IDEO had an incentive to promote the case. Figures and target-audience descriptions vary across later retellings.

sources.title: Bank of America enlists IDEO's services, FTW

title: Office 2007 usage data stopped the team dropping the Paste button
summary: For the Office 2007 redesign (the Ribbon), Microsoft mined opt-in usage data from Office 2003 alongside years of usability testing. The data overturned an internal assumption that the toolbar Paste button was unnecessary, and Paste became the first big button in Word's Ribbon. Usability tests had also shown people rarely clicked unlabeled icons, so Ribbon commands were labeled.
problem: Office had grown to thousands of commands spread across menus, toolbars and task panes. People could not find features, and design debates were driven by guesses and anecdotes about how people used the product.
research: Opt-in telemetry from the Office Customer Experience Improvement Program (SQM), covering all opted-in Word 2003 users and every command run by any means; plus usability testing over several years and early tests of Ribbon prototypes.
insight: Paste alone was over 11% of all Word 2003 commands, more than twice the next (Save), and the top five commands were about 32% of use. Even though many people used Ctrl+V or the context menu, the Paste toolbar button was still the most-clicked button. Usability tests also showed most people don't click unlabeled 16x16 icons beyond the first few.
change: The team dropped an early idea of leaving Cut/Copy/Paste buttons out of the Ribbon and made Paste the first large button on Word's first tab. Ribbon commands were given text labels.
outcome: Jensen Harris writes that the data 'kept us from making a crucial, stupid mistake' that beta testers, being expert users, might not have caught. No post-launch metrics are given.
attribution: Direct: the design lead names the specific decision the data changed.
caveats: Written by Microsoft's own UX lead. Analytics is behavioural data rather than direct observation, though it was paired with usability testing. No outcome metric; the Ribbon itself was controversial with experienced users at launch.

sources.title: No Distaste for Paste (Why the UI, Part 7)

title: Etsy's infinite scroll lost in an A/B test, so the team killed it
summary: Etsy built infinite scroll for search results on the assumption that more items, faster, would help buyers. A controlled test showed the opposite: people saw and clicked fewer items, favorited fewer and bought fewer items from search. Follow-up tests showed the premises behind the feature were wrong, and it was removed.
problem: The team believed showing more search results, faster, would be a better shopping experience, and invested in building infinite scroll before checking whether that belief held.
research: An A/B test of infinite scroll against standard paginated search, followed by a month of checking for browser- and location-specific bugs, then two smaller experiments testing the underlying premises: more results per page, and artificially slower search.
insight: Users with infinite scroll saw fewer items than the control group, clicked fewer, saved fewer favorites and bought fewer items from search (overall purchases held because people found items other ways). Showing more results per page barely changed behaviour and did not increase purchases; adding delay to search changed nothing measurable.
change: Etsy removed infinite scroll ('we took infinite scroll out back and we shot it') and changed its process to validate premises with minimal experiments before building large features.
outcome: A feature that hurt search engagement and search-driven purchases was rolled back. Dan McKinley's talk gives directional results but no percentages; avoided cost is the main win, plus a shift in how Etsy scoped product work.
attribution: Direct: the experiment results were the stated reason for removing the feature.
caveats: First-party conference talk by an Etsy engineer (2012). The win is avoiding a harmful change after it was built, not before. Exact effect sizes are not in the talk transcript; larger percentages circulating in third-party blogs could not be verified. This is experimentation rather than qualitative research.

sources.title: Design for Continuous Experimentation (talk transcript)

title: GE Healthcare redesigns scanners as adventures after seeing children's fear
summary: GE designer Doug Dietz saw a frightened child facing an MRI scan he had designed and realised he had designed the machine, not the experience. Working with children, child-life specialists and children's-museum experts, GE created the 'Adventure Series', themed rooms that turn a scan into a story. Hospitals using it report scanning about 7% more children.
problem: Many young children were too frightened to lie still for MRI and CT scans; Dietz cites about 80% of children aged 3 to 8 needing sedation, which adds risk, time and cost.
research: Input from childhood-learning experts at Milwaukee's Betty Brinn Children's Museum, child-life specialists at children's hospitals, and children themselves in brainstorming sessions. Dietz's starting point was watching families struggle through scans.
insight: The problem was the experience around the machine, not the machine. Children's own ideas shaped themes: a boy said the machines were too noisy, which led to a space-adventure theme where the noise is part of the story; another suggested the table be a sleeping bag ('Cozy Camp').
change: GE created themed scanner rooms (e.g. space, camping, pirate) with a scripted story staff use to guide children through the scan.
outcome: Hospitals using the designs report about a 7% increase in patient volume (scans of children). The Milwaukee Magazine piece gives no sedation or satisfaction figures; an anecdote describes a 6-year-old completing a 40-minute PET/CT scan in the Cozy Camp room.
attribution: The design is clearly a product of the co-design work. The 7% figure is reported by hospitals via GE and is not linked to a specific study.
caveats: Widely retold, often with larger, unsourced claims about sedation dropping sharply and satisfaction rising 90%; those could not be verified from an original source and are excluded here. The 80% baseline is Dietz's own figure without a cited study. Outcome comes from the manufacturer's account.

sources.title: A Scanner Not So Darkly
Scary CT Scans Get a Kid-Friendly Makeover

title: Airbnb doubles weekly revenue after meeting New York hosts and fixing photos
summary: In Airbnb's early days, its New York listings weren't converting. The founders reviewed the listings, saw that the photos were poor, then flew to New York to meet hosts and re-photograph their homes themselves. Weekly revenue reportedly went from $200 to $400.
problem: Growth had stalled for months and New York listings were getting little booking traction.
research: The founders reviewed their roughly 40 New York listings for patterns, then went to New York, visited hosts in person and photographed their places (around 2009).
insight: The listings shared one problem: the photos were bad, so guests couldn't see what they would be paying for. Meeting hosts in person also showed the founders what hosts needed.
change: The founders replaced amateur photos with high-quality ones taken themselves; this later grew into Airbnb's professional photography program for hosts.
outcome: First Round Review reports that better photos doubled weekly revenue from $200 to $400, the first financial improvement in over eight months.
attribution: Founder-told story. The change is clearly linked to what they observed, but there was no control and the timeframe is short.
caveats: This is founder lore retold in many forms (camera cost and details vary). The 'research' was informal: reviewing listings and visiting hosts, not a structured study. Revenue at that scale is noisy. Often cited as a design-thinking or 'do things that don't scale' story rather than a research one.

sources.title: How design thinking transformed Airbnb from a failing startup to a billion dollar business

title: Kaiser Permanente's shift-change redesign got nurses to patients 3x faster
summary: Kaiser Permanente's in-house Innovation Consultancy, which learned human-centered design with IDEO, spent hundreds of hours observing nurses and found that shift changes were a weak point for both information and patient contact. The resulting Nurse Knowledge Exchange redesign moved handoffs toward the bedside. KP reports that in the pilot nurses saw patients at the start of their shift three times faster.
problem: Nurses spent little time at the bedside, and shift changes were chaotic: information was lost between nurses and patients had to wait for the incoming nurse.
research: Over 300 hours of observation of nurses, patients, physicians and support staff, over 20 hours of formal interviews across roles, and a time-and-motion study; followed by storytelling, synthesis, brainstorming, prototyping and field testing on units.
insight: Most of nurses' attention was taken up by the 'system' (documentation, equipment, interruptions) rather than caring for patients, and shift change created hectic starts, especially with patients in pain.
change: Nurse Knowledge Exchange (later NKEplus): structured handoff with patient involvement, a final hourly round before shift change (pain, toileting, positioning, personal items), support staff covering call lights during handoff, and a unit safety check.
outcome: KP's Innovation Consultancy reports that 'nurses got to see patients at the start of their shift 3x faster under NKE pilot'. The model later spread across KP units.
attribution: The redesign came directly out of the observation work. The 3x figure is from a pilot, as reported by the team that designed it.
caveats: Source is a first-party conference deck (2010) with headline figures and no method for the 3x measurement. IDEO's role was teaching the method, so it's sometimes retold as an IDEO project. Pilot results may not hold at scale.

sources.title: Using Human Centered Design to Achieve Operational Impact (Kaiser Permanente Innovation Consultancy, Christi Zuber)
sources.publisher: POMS College of Healthcare Operations Management

title: P&G's Febreze home visits revealed people go 'nose-blind', prompting a relaunch
summary: Febreze launched as an odor eliminator and sold poorly. P&G researchers visiting homes met a woman with nine cats whose house smelled strongly but who couldn't smell it herself, which showed that people stop noticing their own bad smells. P&G repositioned Febreze as a pleasant finishing scent and it became a bestseller.
problem: After millions spent developing a spray that removed odors, sales of the launch campaign (smoky jackets, smelly sofas) were low.
research: Home visits to customers by P&G researchers, as recounted by journalist Charles Duhigg (1990s).
insight: People become desensitized to the smells in their own homes, so they don't feel a need for an odor remover. What they did want was a nice smell after cleaning.
change: P&G repositioned Febreze as an air freshener that adds a pleasant scent at the end of cleaning, rather than a fix for bad smells.
outcome: Priceonomics, citing Duhigg, says the product 'became a bestseller'. Retellings give larger figures (sales doubling within two months; a $1 billion brand) that could not be verified from an accessible original here.
attribution: The insight from home visits is credited with the repositioning. But the commercial turnaround also involved new scents and advertising, and the story comes via a journalist, not P&G data.
caveats: Secondhand: from Duhigg's 2012 New York Times Magazine article and book The Power of Habit, here confirmed via a summary that cites them. P&G has not published the research. Numbers have drifted in retelling; treat as an illustrative classic.

sources.title: Priceonomics summary of the Febreze story (citing Charles Duhigg, NYT)

title: LEGO's four years of research with girls led to LEGO Friends, which doubled sales targets
summary: With about 90% of its consumers boys, LEGO spent roughly four years studying how girls play and testing ideas with them. The resulting LEGO Friends line (2012) used mini-doll figures, named characters and detailed settings. NPR reports it doubled sales expectations in its launch year and sales to girls tripled.
problem: In 2011, 90% of LEGO's consumers were boys, and earlier attempts to sell to girls had not worked.
research: About four years of research into how girls and boys play, including asking girls what they would want in sets (e.g. 'what would you like to see in a Lego school?'). Sample sizes are not given in the NPR report; other sources cite figures from 3,000 to 4,500 girls and mothers that vary between accounts.
insight: When girls build, they tend to play 'on the inside' of a structure and with characters and stories, and they value small, realistic details (an art studio with paint canisters and a canvas, for example).
change: LEGO launched Friends: five named mini-doll characters with storylines and detailed settings such as a vet's office, karate studio and beauty parlour.
outcome: Per NPR: the line 'doubled sales expectations in 2012', the year it launched, and 'sales to girls tripled in just that year'.
attribution: The research shaped the line's design and is widely credited for its success, but launch-year sales also depend on marketing, retail placement and price; no causal analysis is published.
caveats: Sales figures are company statements reported by press. The line was criticized for reinforcing gender stereotypes, so 'success' is commercial, not a verdict on the research framing. Research sample sizes differ across sources.

sources.title: Girls' Legos Are A Hit, But Why Do Girls Need Special Legos?

title: Watching people clean their floors led P&G and Continuum to the Swiffer
summary: P&G asked design firm Continuum to help invent a better mop. Researchers videotaped people cleaning at home and saw how much they hated touching dirty mops, and that most floor dirt was dust that could be picked up electrostatically. The Swiffer launched in 1999 and is reported to have sold more than 11 million starter kits in its first year.
problem: P&G's new-ventures group wanted a better way to clean floors; mops and buckets were messy and disliked.
research: In-home observation and video of people cleaning (late 1990s). Because participants often cleaned before researchers arrived, researchers reportedly started bringing in dirt themselves, for example spilling coffee grounds, to watch real clean-up.
insight: People hated handling dirty mops and wringing them out; much of the dirt was fine dust that could be picked up electrostatically. One older participant swept spilled coffee grounds and then used a damp paper towel for the fine residue rather than a mop.
change: The Swiffer: a lightweight sweeper with disposable electrostatic or wet cloths, sold on a razor-and-blades model.
outcome: Continuum's case study says it generated $100 million in sales in its first four months, more than 11.1 million starter kits sold in the US within a year, and eventually became a $500 million annual brand.
attribution: The product concept is credited to the observation work by both the agency and independent press. Sales also reflect P&G's distribution and marketing power.
caveats: Sales figures come from the design agency's own case study (incentive to promote); independent press (Boston Globe) confirms the research story and calls the product a 'blockbuster' without numbers. The coffee-grounds anecdote appears in marketing retellings without a cited source. P&G has not published current sales.

sources.title: Procter & Gamble customer case study (EPAM Continuum)
In Swiffer, a pet project that went big
Why researchers tricked a woman into cleaning her floor

title: IBM's 1999 site redesign: the much-quoted 'help use down 84%, sales up 400%'
summary: Usage data showed that the most-used features on IBM's late-1990s website were search and then the Help button, signs that people could not navigate the site. IBM redesigned the site around ease of use and relaunched in February 1999. The widely quoted result is that Help use fell 84% and sales rose 400%.
problem: IBM's web presence was a hard-to-navigate maze of separate subsites. Search was the most popular feature because navigation failed, and Help was second because search worked poorly.
research: Analysis of how visitors used the site (feature usage), as described in secondary accounts. The redesign took about 10 weeks and more than 100 employees, at a cost estimated 'in the millions'. Details of any usability testing are not given.
insight: Heavy use of search and Help was a symptom of failed navigation, not a sign those features were working.
change: A site-wide redesign to make IBM's web presence more cohesive and easier to navigate, relaunched February 1999.
outcome: Secondary accounts say: in the first week after the redesign, use of the Help button fell 84% and sales rose 400%. Another account says IBM announced, one month after relaunch, that traffic to the Shop IBM store rose 120% and sales went up 400%.
attribution: Weak. The figures are IBM's own announcement relayed by press; the redesign was large and the research input is thinly described. Sales growth in 1999 e-commerce had many other drivers.
caveats: A staple of 'usability ROI' slide decks, but sources disagree on the timeframe (first week vs. one month). The original source (InfoWorld, 1999) is no longer online; the figures here are confirmed only in secondary academic material citing it. Baselines are not given, so a 400% rise could be from a small base. Treat as folklore with a paper trail, not evidence.

sources.title: User Centered Design works... (lecture slides, citing IBM figures)
Modeling Web Usability Diagnostics on the Basis of Usage Statistics (book chapter, citing Battey, InfoWorld 1999)

title: JSTOR drops plans for a native app after in-the-moment mobile interviews
summary: JSTOR had to decide between building a separate mobile app or a responsive website, and its analytics couldn't show how research moved across devices. Short live interviews with people using JSTOR on phones and tablets showed they often started research on one device and finished on another. JSTOR decided not to build an app and invested in a consistent responsive site plus user accounts.
problem: A product-strategy decision: build a dedicated JSTOR mobile app, or make the website responsive? Analytics could not explain mobile users' wider workflows.
research: Targeted live intercepts of mobile-only visitors (phones and tablets) via Ethnio, inviting them to a 10-minute interview and calling them within 30 minutes of opting in. Participant numbers are not published.
insight: Many participants planned to return later and continue their work on another device, and said a consistent interface across devices mattered for getting their tasks done.
change: JSTOR decided not to build a JSTOR app. It prioritized a consistent responsive web interface and individual user accounts so people could save sources and pick up where they left off.
outcome: A native app build was avoided; effort went into responsive web and accounts. No metrics are reported.
attribution: Direct: the vendor's write-up presents the interview findings as the basis of the decision.
caveats: Published by the research-tool vendor (Ethnio) as a customer story, so it has a promotional angle; undated and without participant counts. No cost-avoided figure.

sources.title: JSTOR (ITHAKA): Taking a leap into targeted mobile intercepts
JSTOR reaches mobile users in 10-minute live interviews with Ethnio

title: UK Department of Health discovery concludes no new consultation product is needed
summary: A six-week discovery into how the Department of Health runs public consultations looked at respondents, organisations that collate responses, and policy makers. The team concluded that the needs could be met by using existing tools better, writing in plain English and communicating throughout policy-making, rather than building a new digital product.
problem: The department wanted to improve digital public consultations and expected the answer to be a new product or service.
research: A 6-week discovery (early 2015) with three user groups: individual respondents, consultation response curators at charities and trade unions, and policy makers. Methods included personas, a prioritized list of user needs (card sorting), sketching and prototyping, a design workshop, and a webinar with agencies and Cabinet Office colleagues. Participant numbers are not given.
insight: Respondents' core need was to put their views across clearly, and the department only accepted text responses; most of the improvement could come from process and content, not new software.
change: The team decided not to build a new product or service, and instead to use existing tools more effectively, write consultations in plain English and keep respondents informed throughout the policy process.
outcome: No new build. The product manager writes that the approach needed 'no hard cash'. No metrics reported.
attribution: Direct: the product manager states the research led to the no-build decision.
caveats: Short first-party blog post with no participant numbers or cost estimate. Whether the process changes improved consultations is not reported.

sources.title: Digital consultations: what we discovered in discovery

title: GDS research finds no need for a central government webchat platform
summary: GDS ran a discovery and alpha to see whether government needed a centrally run webchat component, like GOV.UK Pay or Notify. Research with service users, advisers, managers, service teams and contact centres found no need for a shared component. GDS published patterns and guidance instead and closed the alpha.
problem: Several government service teams were using or considering webchat, and GDS needed to decide whether to build and run a shared webchat platform.
research: A call-out to service teams, then discovery and alpha research (2016) with government and commercial contact centres and four user groups: service users, advisers, managers and service teams. Methods included role play of chat interactions, deliberately breaking user journeys, and screen-reader testing for accessibility.
insight: There was no identified need for a central webchat component. Teams would benefit more from shared service patterns. The research also warned against assuming webchat saves money on its own, and found chat conversations are a useful source of insight into user needs.
change: GDS did not build a webchat platform. It produced patterns and guidance for the Service Manual and a published approach to implementing webchat, then ended the alpha.
outcome: A central platform build was avoided; guidance was published instead. No cost figures given.
attribution: Direct: the GDS post presents the decision as a result of the research.
caveats: First-party. No participant counts or estimate of cost avoided. Platform builds may also have been weighed against other GDS priorities not discussed.

sources.title: Webchat: the journey so far

title: Shelter drops an AI advice chatbot for triage after discovery research
summary: Shelter considered building an AI chatbot to personalise housing advice on its website. Discovery research showed the bigger problem was that people with the most urgent, complex needs struggled to reach advisers, while people with simpler needs preferred talking to someone. Shelter switched to designing triage, asked funders for less money, and launched a simple non-AI journey for low-urgency needs.
problem: Shelter wanted to use digital tools to help more people with housing problems and was considering an AI chatbot that would ask questions and curate advice content.
research: A remote discovery run with two specialist agencies. A follow-on triage discovery (April to August 2021) interviewed 10 team leaders/stakeholders and 11 advisers, analysed 15 helpline calls, 60 webchat transcripts and 7 social media conversations, and interviewed 34 service users.
insight: Helpline and webchat were first-come, first-served, so urgent, complex cases often couldn't get through; only 29% of queries handled were high-priority. A chatbot would not fix this. Many users had only a smartphone with limited credit or a landline, and many had health conditions or disabilities.
change: Shelter moved from a chatbot to a triage approach that prioritises urgent, complex cases for one-to-one advice and points simpler needs to advice content. It applied for less funding to run a triage discovery (a later implementation bid succeeded) and launched a tailored journey for low-urgency needs on its existing site without AI.
outcome: The chatbot build was not pursued. No outcome metrics for triage are reported yet.
attribution: Direct: Shelter's product team says the discovery findings redirected the funding bid and the product.
caveats: First-party charity blog. Outcomes of the triage approach were not published at the time; the 29% figure is a pre-change baseline.

sources.title: The importance of discovery in product opportunity selection
How a discovery phase process helped transform our helpline and webchat services

title: Field research in Nepal redirects the Embrace infant warmer toward home use
summary: A Stanford student team set out to make a low-cost way to keep premature and low-birth-weight babies warm, initially as a device for clinics. Observing rural families in Nepal showed that many babies were far from hospitals and that mothers improvised with blankets, hot-water bottles or light bulbs. The team added an at-home warmer that needs no constant electricity, priced at an expected $100 to $200 versus incubators costing up to $20,000.
problem: Millions of premature and underweight babies die each year in their first weeks, often from hypothermia, and conventional incubators are expensive and need reliable power and trained staff.
research: Field observation of hospitals and rural families in Nepal by the student team (around 2007–2008), followed by clinical trials with mothers.
insight: The need was not only in clinics: rural families far from hospitals tried to keep babies warm with blankets, warm water bottles or light bulbs, which were usually not enough (and bulbs sometimes shattered over babies).
change: Alongside the electrically heated clinic version, the team built a cheaper at-home model heated with warm water, with more safety features and more wax to hold 37°C for longer, including during an emergency trip to hospital. Both use a sleeping-bag pouch with a phase-change wax pad.
outcome: At the time of the source the product was in clinical trials with an expected price of $100–$200, against $1,000–$2,000 for incubators in developing countries. Mothers in trials were reluctant to take babies out, and NGOs in Africa and Asia were sending inquiries. No mortality or deployment figures are given.
attribution: The student newspaper credits observations of rural families' unmet needs with the at-home model. Later impact claims are not covered by this source.
caveats: Often retold as a dramatic pivot 'from incubator to sleeping bag'; the 2010 source describes adding an at-home version to a clinic device rather than abandoning it. Health outcomes are not documented here. Student-newspaper source written while the venture was pre-launch.

sources.title: At-risk babies kept warm by Stanford innovation

title: Usage data of about 0.01% leads Mozilla to remove Firefox Tab Groups
summary: Firefox's Tab Groups (Panorama) feature was buggy, slow and getting in the way of Firefox's multi-process rewrite. Telemetry showed only around 0.01% of users used it. Mozilla removed it, deleting more than 24,000 lines of code, rather than spend the effort to rebuild it.
problem: The team had to decide whether to invest in fixing a large, fragile feature with serious performance problems and flaky tests, which also clashed with the move to separate processes for tabs (electrolysis).
research: Firefox usage telemetry measured over a long period, as part of a 'Great or Dead' review of Firefox features; combined with the bug record.
insight: Usage was extremely low, around 0.01% of users, which could not justify the work needed to bring the feature up to acceptable quality for millions of users.
change: Tab Groups was removed from Firefox (with an add-on path for existing users) instead of being rebuilt.
outcome: More than 24,000 lines of code were removed, freeing the team from maintaining the feature and unblocking multi-process work. Tab groups later returned in a new design years afterwards.
attribution: Usage data was a central reason, alongside quality and architecture problems, so it was one of several causes.
caveats: Written on a Mozilla engineer's personal blog, not an official report. Behavioural analytics only; no qualitative research on why people didn't use it. A small but vocal group of users was upset, and Mozilla later reintroduced tab groups, so the long-term call is debatable.

sources.title: Why was Tab Groups (Panorama) removed?

title: Zillow keeps map beside listings after user feedback, reports up to 8% more agent contacts
summary: While redesigning its search results page, Zillow's UX team gathered customer feedback on several layout variations through UserTesting. Shoppers said they valued seeing the map and the home list side by side, so the team kept that layout. The vendor case study credits it with up to an 8% lift in people contacting real estate agents.
problem: The UX team was redesigning the search results experience and worried a large layout change could hurt conversion (contacts to agents) and revenue.
research: Remote customer feedback sessions run through UserTesting on variations of the search results page, covering map placement, advertising options and how listings were shown. Sample size and dates are not given; the case study PDF dates to about 2019.
insight: Home shoppers relied on geographic context. Many said seeing the map and listings side by side helped them decide whether to inquire about a home.
change: Zillow launched a search results layout that kept the map and the list of homes side by side.
outcome: The case study says the map inclusion produced 'up to an 8 percent lift' in customers reaching out to real estate agents, which it says boosted revenue. No dollar figure is given.
attribution: The vendor ties the conversion lift directly to the feedback-informed layout, but does not say how the lift was measured or whether other changes shipped at the same time.
caveats: Vendor marketing piece written by UserTesting about its own client. 'Up to' 8% is a ceiling, not an average. No method for the conversion measurement, no sample size, no control group described. Zillow's own publications do not appear to document this.

sources.title: Zillow improves home search experience, increasing conversion by 8 percent
Case Study: Zillow achieves an 8% conversion lift and improved home-search experience with UserTesting

title: Costco Travel drops a single 'Vacation Packages' entry after testers couldn't book; support calls fall 82%
summary: Costco Travel planned to let members build their own trip packages through one search entry point in the main navigation. Prototype testing showed visitors could not complete a hotel-plus-flight booking that way, so the team moved to multiple entry points after about 20 tests. The vendor reports more bookings and 82% fewer support calls after launch.
problem: Costco Travel wanted members to build their own travel packages online. Most of the team favored a single entry point, a search widget labeled 'Vacation Packages', in the main navigation.
research: The web accessibility and UX lead built prototypes of the team's top ideas and tested them remotely with website visitors on UserTesting, alongside a review of competitor sites. In total about 20 tests over 6 rounds, covering layouts, icons, radio buttons and search fields. Participant counts and dates are not given.
insight: The single 'Vacation Packages' entry point did not match how visitors thought about the task. When asked to show how they would book a hotel and flight, testers 'simply could not complete the task.'
change: The team abandoned the single entry point and offered several entry points into package building, then refined the details through further rounds of testing.
outcome: According to the case study, bookings of customer-built travel rose in the weeks after launch (no figure given) and support calls decreased by 82%.
attribution: The research directly overturned the team's preferred design, which is well documented. The 82% support-call drop is reported without baseline, time window or method, so the link from research to that number is asserted rather than shown.
caveats: Vendor case study written by UserTesting about its own customer. No participant numbers, no measurement period for the 82% figure, no booking numbers. Undated; mentions COVID-era travel restrictions, so likely 2020-2022.

sources.title: How Costco Travel built a better online travel booking experience
Case Study: Costco Travel achieves intuitive online bookings and 82% fewer support calls with UserTesting

title: American Airlines benchmarks booking and trip management, lifts completion of key tasks 37%
summary: American Airlines set up a UX benchmarking program, scoring its booking, trip management, check-in and loyalty experiences with potential customers and against competing airlines. Tests showed people could not find where to add passport details, loyalty numbers or meal requests. After the trip-management flows were reworked, the vendor reports a 37% rise in completion for those tasks.
problem: The team wanted to understand how customers actually used booking and self-service features, beyond analytics and internal assumptions, and needed a shared measure of experience quality.
research: Benchmark usability studies with potential customers on UserTesting covering four journeys (booking, changing/managing a flight, check-in, AAdvantage), scored with the vendor's QXscore and compared with competing airlines. Click tests and heat maps were used on the booking path. Sample sizes not given; around 2023.
insight: Customers struggled to find where to enter passport information, add a loyalty account, request a meal or email an itinerary. Heat maps also showed the multi-city search option sat below the fold where searchers missed it.
change: The UX team reworked the change-and-manage-trip concepts so these tasks were easier to find, and re-measured them in the benchmark.
outcome: The case study reports a 15% average increase in QXscore across the experiences measured and changed, and a 37% increase in customer completion rate for the updated tasks (passport details, loyalty accounts, meal requests, emailing itineraries).
attribution: Before/after benchmark scores on the same tasks tie the improvement to the redesign that the research prompted. No control group, and no live business metric is reported.
caveats: Vendor case study. QXscore is UserTesting's proprietary metric. Completion is measured in test sessions, not in live traffic. No baseline values, sample sizes or statistical detail. The multi-city finding has no reported change or result.

sources.title: American Airlines customer story
Case Study: American Airlines achieves a 15% average increase in QXscore with UserTesting

title: Spabreaks.com usability testing finds booking-funnel fixes; conversion up 28% within six months
summary: Spabreaks.com, a small UK spa-booking site, hired Clearleft for a three-week discovery focused on its conversion funnel. Usability testing, an expert review and analytics showed the site didn't support how visitors browsed before booking, and the team shipped a set of prioritised quick wins. Comparing before and after, the agency reports a 28% rise in conversion rate and 78% more booking revenue within six months.
problem: A small team with limited resources had a growing backlog and no way to prioritise it. They suspected the site was built around booking and did not support visitors' earlier browsing behaviour.
research: Three-week discovery by Clearleft (published around 2019): interviews with 13 stakeholders from eight departments, an expert review, a competitor assessment, Google Analytics analysis to pick high-traffic, high-bounce pages, and moderated usability testing of key pages with Spabreaks staff observing. Findings were prioritised with dot voting.
insight: Customer concerns shifted along the journey: early visitors were browsing and comparing, but the design mostly served people ready to book, so needs near the start of the funnel went unmet.
change: The team implemented a set of quick-win fixes to the conversion funnel and received longer-term design recommendations. The case study does not list the specific changes.
outcome: Comparing data from before the changes, Clearleft reports 'a 28% increase in conversion rate and 78% increase in revenue from bookings within 6 months.' The managing director also cites more online bookings and lower bounce rates on key pages.
attribution: The client's marketing manager credits the quick wins from the research for the conversion increase, but the six-month window would include seasonality, marketing and any other site changes.
caveats: Agency case study about its own client. Before/after only, no control group. Doesn't say whether 28% is relative or in percentage points, and gives no baseline. Specific changes not described. Revenue growth over six months likely reflects factors beyond the site.

sources.title: Spabreaks.com case study

title: Multi-store retailer applies checkout usability research, reports checkout conversion doubled
summary: An ecommerce business running several specialist online stores applied Baymard Institute's checkout usability guidelines, which come from Baymard's large-scale usability testing, across all its storefronts. The retailer reported a 100% increase in checkout conversion. Baymard published the account without naming the client or describing the changes.
problem: The retailer's checkout across several specialist stores was underperforming and it wanted research-backed guidance on what to fix.
research: No new studies of the retailer's own customers. The team applied Baymard's Ecommerce Checkout Usability guidelines, which Baymard derives from its own usability testing of checkout flows, covering step order, form labels, button wording, payment confidence and error recovery.
insight: Existing usability research on checkout friction (form design, step order, payment trust, error recovery) applied to the retailer's checkouts, which had violated several of the guidelines.
change: The guideline recommendations were implemented across every store's checkout. The specific design changes are not described.
outcome: The retailer reported a '100% increase in checkout conversion rates', i.e. checkout conversion roughly doubled.
attribution: Weak. The research is generic third-party research, not studies of this retailer's users, and the outcome is a self-reported number with no method.
caveats: Promotional post from the research vendor. Client unnamed, so it can't be checked. No baseline, timeframe, measurement method or list of changes. A doubling usually means a very poor starting point. Include only as an example of applying published research, not as a controlled result.

sources.title: Online Retailer Doubles Checkout Conversion With Baymard

title: Co-op lab tests show members didn't know they could pick a local cause; one-line copy fix lifts selections 10%
summary: Co-op's membership team saw in website feedback and analytics that many members reached the page for the '1% for your community' reward but never chose a cause. Think-aloud lab sessions showed people didn't realise the choice was theirs and didn't notice the clickable element. A small content change, checked in the lab first, was followed by an early 10% rise in members selecting a cause.
problem: Members are meant to choose a local cause to receive 1% of their spending, but many who reached the relevant page didn't select one.
research: Late 2016, Co-op Membership user researchers combined analysis of 9,469 website feedback comments, follow-up phone interviews, short online surveys, analytics on page visits and errors, and think-aloud lab sessions where participants did tasks such as registering a card and choosing a local cause.
insight: People didn't realise they could pick the cause themselves. Some thought Co-op chose for them or that they'd send their choice by email later, and they overlooked the clickable element on screen.
change: A content-only fix: the line 'See your local causes' was added inside the 'your community' box. It was tested in the lab, where participants then understood what to do, before going live.
outcome: Early results after release showed 'a 10% increase in people selecting a cause'.
attribution: Direct. The change came from a specific lab finding, backed by feedback comments and analytics, and was the only change described. Measurement appears to be before/after live data.
caveats: Early results only, reported a week after launch. Measurement method not stated (no A/B test mentioned) and no baseline given, so it isn't clear what the 10% is relative to. First-party blog.

sources.title: How user research is helping us improve the membership site

title: Jet.com shopper tests reveal hunt for shipping and returns info; surfacing it lifts conversion about 10%
summary: Jet.com ran remote user tests with shoppers as soon as new features went live. Recordings showed shoppers kept searching product pages for shipping costs, return policies and how to reach customer service. Jet moved that information onto product detail pages, and its research director described a 'significant' conversion increase of roughly 10% or more.
problem: Jet.com, a young online retailer, wanted to raise conversion on product detail pages and understand where shoppers hesitated.
research: Remote unmoderated usability tests on UserTesting with consumers shopping the live site, typically launched as soon as a new feature shipped (reported in 2016).
insight: Shoppers regularly went looking for supporting information before buying: shipping costs, how to contact customer service, and return policies.
change: Jet placed shipping costs, customer service availability and hours, and related policy information prominently on product detail pages.
outcome: Jet did not disclose exact figures. Research director Ben Babcock described a 'significant' conversion increase of roughly 10 percent or more.
attribution: The research director links the change directly to the shopper-testing finding, but the conversion figure is an approximate verbal estimate with no stated method.
caveats: Secondhand: PYMNTS summarises an Internet Retailer article quoting Jet's research lead. No exact numbers, method or timeframe. Jet.com was a fast-changing young site (later absorbed by Walmart), so other changes could have contributed.

sources.title: Jet.com's Secret Sauce To Improved Conversion Rates

title: Panera's catering site prototype tests fix retail/catering confusion; revenue per visit up 18% year over year
summary: Panera tested clickable prototypes of a new catering ordering site with loyalty members and non-members. Visitors couldn't tell retail from catering, got stuck in a two-page setup and wanted to see customization options and past orders easily. After the redesign the vendor reports a 1.2% conversion bump at launch and, year over year, 18% higher revenue per visit and 9% higher conversion.
problem: Panera was overhauling its catering website, including how guests start, customize and manage large orders, and wanted to avoid building something that confused customers.
research: Around 2024, Panera's product and UX team ran unmoderated usability tests of clickable Figma prototypes on UserTesting, covering order setup and checkout, with participants of varied socioeconomic status and gender, both loyalty members and non-members. Heat maps showed where people clicked.
insight: Some visitors didn't know whether they were on the retail or catering site. People clicked a plain text headline, which suggested the two-page setup should be one page. Customers wanted customization options visible, quicker access to past orders, and frequent orderers such as office administrators valued bundles.
change: Added tabs to switch between retail and catering, with subtle colour differences; merged the two-page setup into one page; highlighted options like half sandwich/half salad; made past orders easier to reach; added bundles and sandwich assortments for one-click large orders.
outcome: The case study reports a '1.2% increase in conversion' from the first round of changes at launch, plus an 18% year-over-year increase in revenue per visit and a 9% year-over-year increase in conversion.
attribution: The changes map clearly onto specific test findings. The year-over-year numbers are before/after and could include pricing, menu, marketing or seasonal effects.
caveats: Vendor case study by UserTesting. No baseline values, sample sizes or measurement details. Year-over-year comparison has no control group. Only the small 1.2% launch figure is tied closely to the first set of changes.

sources.title: Panera Bread customer story

title: Zalando team drops computer-vision search idea after customer research shows outfit hunts start on social media
summary: A group of Zalando intrapreneurs set out to use computer vision to improve search. Before building, they interviewed customers about how they look for outfits and mapped the journey. Most started on social media and used makeshift workarounds to find similar items, which 'changed the course of the whole project' toward redesigning that journey.
problem: An internal innovation team wanted to explore computer vision as a way to improve fashion search, a technology-first starting point.
research: In Zalando's intrapreneurship programme (around 2017-2018) the team wrote a research question about how people search for outfits, met 'several' customers, and turned the conversations into a user journey map.
insight: Most users began their outfit search on social media and then used 'hacky ways' to find similar pieces to buy, so the real problem sat in the jump from inspiration to shopping rather than in search technology.
change: The team changed the project's direction from a computer-vision search tool to redesigning the inspiration-to-purchase journey so users could get there with less effort.
outcome: No metrics. The author describes the result as a 'different approach, huge impact!' for the project's direction.
attribution: Direct for the decision: the post says the research finding itself changed the project's course. Nothing is reported about what shipped afterwards.
caveats: Short first-party blog post used to illustrate an innovation process. Number of customers and methods are vague ('several'). No outcome data, and it isn't clear whether the redesigned journey launched.

sources.title: The Intrapreneurship Journey at Zalando

title: Zalando research finds half of shoppers don't understand 'sustainable fashion'; it launches browsing by cause
summary: Zalando's 'It Takes Two' research found that while most customers call sustainability important, about one in two don't understand what it means in fashion, and complexity and trust block them. In response, Zalando built a browsing experience where customers shop by causes such as animal welfare or water conservation, translating technical sustainability criteria into plain impact areas.
problem: Many customers said sustainability mattered to them, but far fewer acted on it when buying fashion. Zalando wanted to understand the gap and make sustainable products easier to choose.
research: The 'It Takes Two' attitude-behaviour gap study (published 2021) ran in three stages, including a 12-person ethnographic study and a survey of 2,500 consumers across two generations and five markets, plus Zalando's own customer data.
insight: Complexity was a main barrier: roughly one in two customers didn't understand what sustainability means in fashion. Trust was the other blocker, and customers needed a positive, emotional connection to the topic before digging deeper.
change: Zalando launched a value-based browsing experience in the Fashion Store, mapping its existing sustainability criteria onto six cause areas (animal welfare, reusing materials, worker well-being, water conservation, reducing emissions, extending the life of fashion) described in simpler language.
outcome: No outcome metrics reported. Zalando described the launch as a first step and a learning opportunity.
attribution: The launch post explicitly ties the design approach (plain-language cause areas) to the research finding about complexity. No evidence about whether it changed behaviour.
caveats: First-party announcement, partly sustainability communications. No adoption or conversion data. The ethnographic component is small (12 people) and the survey is self-reported attitudes.

sources.title: Zalando Enables More Customers to Shop Sustainably With New Value-Based Browsing Experience
Attitude-Behavior Gap Report

title: Just Eat watches people order at home, splits accordion checkout into pages; order completion up 5%
summary: A designer working on Just Eat's UK site watched people place real takeaway orders in a lab and in their own homes. They got stuck in the single-page accordion checkout, scrolling up and down to open and close panels. The checkout was rebuilt with one step and one button per page, and the designer reports a 5% rise in order completion, plus 3% from a related search results redesign.
problem: Just Eat's checkout was a single-page accordion with inconsistent controls, and the mobile search results page had no filters and an awkward sort control.
research: Around 2014, observation of users placing real orders in a research lab and in their own homes, plus bi-weekly A/B tests in Optimizely used to prioritise work. Participant numbers not stated.
insight: In the accordion checkout people got stuck and scrolled up and down to open and close panels. Controls were inconsistent: the delivery step had several buttons while other steps used radio buttons and a single button.
change: Each checkout step moved to its own page with a single button. Separately, search results got an accessible, responsive sort control that works on all screen sizes, and mobile filters and sort start collapsed so results get more room.
outcome: The designer reports that the multi-page checkout increased order completion rate by 5%, and the search results redesign increased order completion rate by 3%.
attribution: The checkout change responds directly to the observed problem. The team was running regular Optimizely A/B tests, so the figures may come from controlled tests, but the write-up doesn't say so explicitly.
caveats: Written by the designer (a contractor) about his own work, as a portfolio case study, not by Just Eat. Measurement method, baseline and sample sizes aren't given. Old (around 2014). Rated 'measured' rather than 'tested' because the test design isn't stated.

sources.title: Redesigning Just Eat's checkout and search results page

title: Time4Sleep finds bed shoppers lost and missing buying guides; A/B-tested category page lifts mobile conversion 63%
summary: UK bed retailer Time4Sleep and its CRO agency Epiphany combined analytics, session recordings, heatmaps and on-page polls to work out why mobile shoppers weren't buying. Visitors bounced between the beds category and product pages, never found the buried buying guides, and were confused about bed-buying basics even with items in the cart. A redesigned category page, A/B tested against two other variants, produced a 63% rise in mobile conversion for bed shoppers.
problem: About 70% of Time4Sleep's traffic was mobile, and mobile visitors weren't converting well, especially in the beds category.
research: Around 2017, the agency queried Google Analytics for back-and-forth paths between category and product pages, watched session recordings of those visitors, studied mobile heatmaps, and ran on-page polls asking things like 'Is there anything preventing you from purchasing at this point?' Persona work suggested first-time bed buyers lacked basic knowledge. Some remote user test videos were also run but proved less useful.
insight: Visitors reached checkout with a product in the cart but still lacked information to finish. They looped between the bed category page and product pages, rarely clicked buying-guide links because they were buried under other content, and rarely used sort buttons because it wasn't clear what they did. Poll answers confirmed confusion about bed-buying fundamentals.
change: The beds category page got visible links to information pages (size guides, children's bed guides) at the top, simpler filters for mobile, and improved informational content. Three variations were built and A/B tested.
outcome: The winning variation produced 'a 63% increase in mobile conversion rates for the bed shopper segment'. For the Beds category page the case study also reports a 19% increase in overall conversions, 36% more visitors reaching the cart, 124% more visitors reaching informational content, and a 9% reduction in category-page bounce rate.
attribution: Strong for a vendor story: the change came from specific research findings and was A/B tested against the existing page. The 63% applies to one segment (mobile bed shoppers), not the whole site.
caveats: Published by Hotjar (the tool vendor) with the CRO agency, both with an incentive. Test duration, sample size and significance aren't reported. Much of the 'research' is behavioural analytics plus short polls rather than moderated studies; the team said its user-test videos weren't very helpful. Exact year is approximate.

sources.title: Time4Sleep made mobile conversions skyrocket—and you can, too!
Case Study: Time4Sleep achieves 63% increase in mobile conversions with Hotjar

title: Intertop exit survey shows shoppers can't finish the checkout form; simplified form lifts conversion 54.68% in A/B test
summary: Ukrainian shoe retailer Intertop was losing almost half of shoppers at checkout. Its agency, Turum-burum, put an exit-intent survey on the checkout page: of 444 respondents, 48.6% said they couldn't complete the order form. A shorter, blocked-out form with autofill raised checkout conversion 54.68% in an A/B test, and average revenue per user rose 11.46% after rollout.
problem: Almost half of prospective customers abandoned Intertop's checkout, and the team didn't know why.
research: An exit-intent pop-up survey on the checkout page asked 'Why would you like to stop placing the order?' (444 respondents), alongside session recordings and heatmaps showing friction such as rage clicks. Run by the UX/CRO agency Turum-burum.
insight: 48.6% of respondents said they were leaving because they couldn't complete the checkout form. Heatmaps also showed the 'Buy now' button sat below the fold for most users on the product page.
change: Checkout fields were cut to three, the order page was split into clear blocks, and autofill was added for signed-in users. The product page was also simplified so the buy button was visible.
outcome: In the A/B test the variant's conversion rate rose 54.68%. After rollout, average revenue per user grew 11.46% and the checkout bounce rate fell 13.35%.
attribution: Direct: the survey pinpointed the form as the barrier, the changes targeted it, and the variant was A/B tested against the original.
caveats: Reported by the analytics vendor (Hotjar/Contentsquare) about an agency client; both have an incentive. Test length, traffic and significance aren't given. The 54.68% applies to the checkout step, not site-wide conversion. Survey is self-reported by people already leaving. Source undated; year is approximate.

sources.title: A/B testing examples (Turum-burum for Intertop)

title: Instacart field research with in-store shoppers leads to one-handed app design and one-tap substitution messages
summary: Instacart's design team observed shoppers in grocery stores and shopped orders themselves to audit the experience. They saw that shoppers are always moving, with one hand on a cart or a product, and that out-of-stock items drive most of the back-and-forth with customers. That led to a one-handed Shopper app and features such as photo-backed messages and one-tap approval of replacement items.
problem: Instacart shoppers work in busy stores carrying up to 50,000 products whose stock Instacart doesn't control, and the team needed the Shopper app to fit real in-store conditions and keep customers informed.
research: Field research observing Instacart shoppers in stores and how they handled different scenarios, plus first-hand shopping by designers to audit the journey (described in 2021).
insight: Shoppers usually use the phone with one hand while the other pushes a cart or picks items. Missing items are inevitable, and good communication matters more than perfection: customers still give 5-star ratings when the shopper clearly tried their best.
change: A simplified, one-handed Shopper app with large icons, big tap targets and fewer manual inputs; prompts asking customers for replacement preferences on low-stock items; quick messaging with shelf photos; context such as first-time customer flags; crowdsourced out-of-stock data that stops later customers adding the item; and auto-generated substitution messages customers can approve with one tap.
outcome: No numbers. Instacart says automated messaging cuts back-and-forth for both shopper and customer and that ratings data supports the value of communication.
attribution: The post presents the one-handed principle and the communication features as direct results of field observation, but gives no outcome data.
caveats: First-party design blog written partly for recruiting. No participant numbers, dates or metrics. Some features (crowdsourced stock data) rely on analytics as much as research.

sources.title: Designing Digital Experiences That Augment the Analog World

title: Despegar's pandemic traveler research backs flexible packages and kills the hard sell
summary: When COVID-19 upended travel, Latin American online travel agency Despegar stepped up surveys and interviews with frequent travelers and tested hotel photo sets. Travelers were uncertain about income and trips, disliked aggressive sales tactics, and reacted badly to sanitation photos of rooms and food. The team made flexible cancellation and packages core products, softened its tone against stakeholder pressure for a hard sell, and changed how sanitation imagery is shown.
problem: Travel demand and traveler attitudes changed abruptly in 2020, and the team needed to know what travelers in different Latin American markets felt and wanted before deciding product and messaging.
research: In 2020 the UX research team ran self-reported surveys and interviews with frequent travelers recruited through social media and groups (past bookers were excluded because many were trying to cancel), and tested two hotel photo sets: standard amenity photos versus photos emphasising sanitation.
insight: Many travelers were unsure about trips and their future income, reacted poorly to aggressive sales tactics, and split into risk-averse and risk-tolerant groups. Sanitation photos of intimate spaces like rooms and food caused discomfort, while communal spaces like lobbies did not. Attitudes differed by country (Brazil and Mexico readier to travel than Argentina), and six in ten planned a first trip within their own country.
change: Flexible cancellation and modification features, and flexible packages, became core products. The team pushed back on stakeholders who wanted a hard sell and moved to a softer, reassuring voice. Supplier sanitation imagery was guided toward communal spaces rather than rooms and food.
outcome: No business metrics reported. The team says flexible packages became the most popular option despite higher prices, and flexibility features became core products.
attribution: The NN/g article, based on interviews with Despegar's UX and research leads, credits the research with the tone change and the imagery guidance. The rise of flexible packages was also driven by the pandemic itself, so research is one of several causes.
caveats: Secondhand account from NN/g interviews with the company's own UX leads. Mostly self-reported attitudes gathered during a crisis. No metrics on bookings, conversion or revenue.

sources.title: COVID-19 Has Changed Your Users

title: Property Finder sees evening browsers reluctant to phone agents, launches WhatsApp enquiries
summary: UAE property portal Property Finder combined periodic user surveys (over 1,500 users across 18 months) with other discovery research. One finding was that mobile users browse heavily in the evening but hesitate to call agents. That led to a test of WhatsApp as a way to contact agents, which the company says reached 'almost instant product-market fit'.
problem: The portal wanted more buyers and renters to contact agents, and needed to understand how and when people searched and what stopped them reaching out.
research: Around 2019: periodic sentiment surveys of more than 1,500 portal users over about a year and a half, plus discovery work the team describes as personas, diary studies and user interviews, and a map of more than 40 questions buyers and renters ask during a search.
insight: Mobile users were very active in the evening but reluctant to phone agents. Research also showed some information (popular unit types, guest parking, community issues) is best supplied by residents, and that the map is central to the UAE search journey.
change: Property Finder tested and launched WhatsApp Leads, a way to message agents instead of calling. Related findings led to resident-written Community Guides, Building Reviews on listing pages, and better map search.
outcome: The company says WhatsApp Leads reached 'almost instant product-market fit'. No lead numbers are given. Separately, it reports over 10% of mobile searches used Map Search.
attribution: The post states the evening-browsing finding 'inspired' the WhatsApp test. The success claim is qualitative.
caveats: First-party blog by a product manager, published in 2023 about 2019 work. No lead volumes, conversion or test design reported. The specific research method behind the WhatsApp insight isn't separated from the general list of methods.

sources.title: Property portals redesigned

title: Rightmove builds Shared Lists after home hunters repeatedly ask for it in user testing
summary: Rightmove, the UK's largest property portal, launched Shared Lists, which let renters and buyers collect listings and send them to others who can react, comment and suggest alternatives. Its CTO said the idea was 'repeatedly requested during thousands of hours of user testing'.
problem: Buyers and renters had no built-in way on Rightmove to share a shortlist of listings with other people and discuss it.
research: Ongoing user testing sessions with renters and buyers, described as 'thousands of hours' in total, in which participants kept asking for a way to share and discuss shortlists. Details of method and sample aren't published.
insight: Participants in user testing kept asking for a way to share and discuss listings with others inside the product.
change: Rightmove launched Shared Lists in November 2025 for both renters and buyers: users build collections of agents' listings and share them, and recipients can react, comment and propose alternatives.
outcome: No usage or business metrics reported at launch.
attribution: The company directly credits user testing as the source of the idea. Nothing yet shows whether it changed behaviour.
caveats: Trade-press report of a launch announcement. 'Thousands of hours' is unspecific and refers to user testing in general, not a dedicated study. No outcome data.

sources.title: Rightmove rolls out Shared Lists to help renters and buyers' search

title: Chrome's research-based SSL warning got about 30% more people to stay safe
summary: Chrome's security warnings for bad HTTPS connections were widely misunderstood and clicked through. Google researchers redesigned the warning using warning-science guidance, checked comprehension with microsurveys, and ran a field experiment. Adherence rose from 37% to 62%, though comprehension barely improved.
problem: Most people who saw Chrome's SSL/TLS warning ignored it and proceeded to potentially dangerous sites, and few understood what the warning meant.
research: Google security and UX researchers (with a University of Pennsylvania collaborator) designed candidate warnings from published warning-design recommendations, measured comprehension with online microsurveys, and compared warning versions in a field experiment with real Chrome users. Published at CHI 2015.
insight: Simplifying the language (to roughly sixth-grade reading level) did not make people understand the threat much better. What did change behavior was 'opinionated design': visual cues and layout that make the safe choice the obvious one and make proceeding harder to find.
change: Chrome shipped a new warning with simpler text, a stronger visual treatment, and the 'proceed anyway' path de-emphasized behind an extra step.
outcome: In the field, adherence (users choosing not to proceed) rose from 37% to 62% (reported as 61% in some coverage). The authors state plainly that they failed at their goal of a well-understood warning.
attribution: Direct. The research team designed, tested, and shipped the warning, and the field experiment compares warning versions.
caveats: Comprehension did not meaningfully improve, so the win is behavioral, not understanding. Figures reported as 61% or 62% depending on the outlet. Authors are Google employees writing about Google's product, though in a peer-reviewed venue. 2015.

sources.title: Improving SSL Warnings: Comprehension and Adherence
Google Improves Chrome's SSL Warnings

title: Facebook's compassion research made more people ask friends to take photos down
summary: Facebook found that many reported photos weren't policy violations but embarrassing pictures posted by friends. Working with UC Berkeley and Yale emotion researchers, it redesigned the reporting flow to help people message the poster in emotionally specific language. Message sending, photo removal and replies all went up.
problem: Large numbers of users reported photos to Facebook that broke no rules (unflattering or embarrassing pictures of themselves). Facebook couldn't act on them, and the old flow left users to write their own message to the poster, which few did.
research: Facebook's team led by Arturo Bejar reviewed flagged photos and the reporting flow, and partnered with UC Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center (Dacher Keltner, Paul Piff, Emiliana Simon-Thomas) on emotion-based message design. Yale's Center for Emotional Intelligence ran focus groups with 13–14-year-olds and interviewed kids who had been cyberbullied. New flows were piloted on a random 50% of US English-language users.
insight: People reporting these photos wanted the friend to remove it, not Facebook to punish anyone. They were much more likely to reach out when helped to name how the content made them feel and given polite, personal wording. Teens related to 'this post is a problem' more than to the word 'report'.
change: The adult flow asked 'I don't like this photo because:' with emotion-based options and pre-filled, polite messages naming the friend. For teens, 'Report' became 'This post is a problem', with more specific reasons and an option to message a trusted adult.
outcome: With generic default text, message sending rose from 20% to 51%. In the new flow, about 75–80% sent the suggested message; half of content creators deleted the photo (versus a third under the old system); about 75% replied, a nearly 50% increase. Teens contacting a trusted adult went from 19% to 43%.
attribution: Strong. The redesigned flows came directly out of the research partnership and were compared with the old flow in a pilot.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2012 magazine article published by one of the research partners (Greater Good), relaying Facebook's figures; some are preliminary. Exact comparison method for each number isn't detailed. Old (2011–2012).

sources.title: Can Science Make Facebook More Compassionate?

title: Research with parents and photographers put a shutter button on Google's AI camera
summary: Google Clips was meant to be a fully automatic AI camera. Research with photographers and parents, plus prototype testing on users' own footage, showed people needed control and to understand what the camera was looking for. The team added a capture button and viewfinder and deliberately showed more clips than the model rated best.
problem: The team needed to define what a 'memorable moment' is so an on-device model could capture it, and to decide how much control users should have over an automatic camera.
research: Over roughly three years, the team hired a documentary filmmaker, a photojournalist and a fine-art photographer to articulate what makes a good moment, studied parents (especially new parents) and their photo habits, and prototyped the experience with users' real content before the models were finished ('fake it till you make it').
insight: Perfect automatic capture isn't achievable for something this subjective. Users needed a sense of authorship and control. The team's own enthusiasm for futuristic, gesture-heavy interfaces had hidden how complex they would be for real users. Teaching the model what to ignore (fingers over lens, blur, inside a pocket) mattered as much as what to capture.
change: Added a hardware capture button and a software viewfinder; let users choose the still frame and clip length; simplified the UI; had the camera slightly over-deliver clips so users could delete and learn what it looks for; kept processing on-device.
outcome: No metric reported. The research changed core product decisions about user control and interface design.
attribution: The design lead attributes the control features and simplified UI directly to the human-centered research process.
caveats: No outcome metric. Google Clips was discontinued in 2019, so these decisions did not make it a commercial success. Account is first-party (Google Design) plus press coverage of it.

sources.title: The UX of AI
Pro photographers teach Google Clips when (and when not) to take a photo

title: Riot's behavioral research raised League of Legends reform rates to 92%
summary: Riot built a player-behavior team of scientists and designers to study toxicity in League of Legends. They found most bad behavior came from ordinary players having a bad day, not dedicated trolls, and that clear, fast feedback changed behavior. Reform rates rose from 50% to 65% with evidence-backed feedback and to 92% once feedback arrived within minutes.
problem: Abusive chat was widespread in League of Legends, hurting player experience, and banning a small set of 'trolls' wasn't working.
research: A team including PhDs in cognitive neuroscience and human factors, led by Jeffrey Lin, built behavior profiles from game data, ran in-game experiments (optional cross-team chat; a 5×3×4 factorial 'priming' experiment on loading-screen messages), and used the community Tribunal's judgments to train language models. Work presented at GDC 2013 and reported in 2015.
