insight: Severe, consistent toxicity is rare; many toxic games come from otherwise normal players on a bad day, and negativity spreads. Players reform more when they're told exactly what they did, with evidence, and quickly.
change: Made cross-team chat optional; sent banned players 'reform cards' explaining the offense with chat-log evidence; automated detection so feedback arrived within five minutes instead of up to a week; tested priming messages on loading screens.
outcome: Making cross-team chat optional significantly reduced offensive language, obscenity and negative attitude. Reform rates rose from 50% to 65% after adding better feedback and evidence, and to an all-time high of 92% with near-instant feedback. Community Tribunal verdicts matched Riot's internal team 98% of the time.
attribution: Fairly direct: the interventions were designed from the team's behavioral findings, and some were run as in-game experiments.
caveats: Figures come from Riot staff in talks and interviews; methods behind each number aren't published. Different outlets report different percentages. 'Reform' is Riot's own definition (not reoffending). The priming experiment results were only partially shared. One finding (a red positive question) backfired.

sources.title: A Video-Game Algorithm to Solve Online Abuse
GDC: Riot experimentally investigates online toxicity

title: 3,000 hours of lab playtesting reshaped Halo 3's levels and weapons
summary: Microsoft's games user research lab watched about 600 ordinary players for more than 3,000 hours of Halo 3, combining video, think-aloud, in-game ratings and telemetry heat maps. The data exposed players getting lost, wasting ammo and killing themselves with a tank turret, and designers fixed each issue.
problem: Bungie needed to know whether Halo 3's campaign and multiplayer maps played as intended for everyday players, not just expert staff.
research: Led by Randy Pagulayan, starting fall 2006: roughly 20 players every other week, about 600 in total, more than 3,000 hours of play. Methods included one-way-mirror observation, face and controller video, think-aloud, pop-up prompts asking players to rate fun or frustration, and telemetry turned into location and death heat maps.
insight: Location maps showed players wandering aimlessly in the jungle level; players fired at out-of-range enemies; AI marines grabbed the Warthogs before players could; players aimed the Wraith turret low and blew themselves up; a death heat map showed one base on the Valhalla map had an advantage.
change: Added one-way ledges so players couldn't backtrack in the jungle; made the reticle turn red when enemies were in range; added more Warthogs; limited how low the Wraith turret could aim; reshaped Valhalla's terrain; rebalanced ammo, grenades and melee.
outcome: Follow-up telemetry showed players moving through the jungle level as intended. In later ratings, 52% of players gave that level 5 out of 5 for fun and 40% gave it 4. Some issues (finding the melee button, one cliff route) were still unresolved at the time of writing.
attribution: Direct for each fix: the article ties specific design changes to specific playtest observations.
caveats: Journalism based on access to the lab, not a published study. The fun ratings are from playtesters, not a before/after comparison with a baseline. 2007. The full Wired text was read via an archived copy because wired.com blocked automated fetching.

sources.title: Halo 3: How Microsoft Labs Invented a New Science of Play
Halo 3: How Microsoft Labs Invented a New Science of Play (archived copy)
The process of testing Halo3

title: Gamers with limited mobility shaped the Xbox Adaptive Controller's one-hand packaging
summary: Microsoft wanted packaging that people with limited dexterity could open with one hand. A design researcher consulted gamers and disability advocates, and designers tested prototypes with employees and gamers with limited mobility. Specific findings like 'no teeth' and oval loops went straight into the final box.
problem: Standard packaging (twist ties, plastic clamshells, lids needing two hands) is hard or impossible to open for many people with disabilities, the exact audience for the Adaptive Controller.
research: Xbox design researcher Scott Wang consulted gamers and disability advocates during controller development. Packaging designer Mark Weiser reviewed existing accessible packaging and tested prototypes (over 100 iterations of components, three finalists) with Microsoft employees with limited mobility and gamers in the US and UK, watching them open the boxes. 2018.
insight: Many disabled gamers open packaging with their teeth and wanted that never to be necessary. People preferred more simple steps over fewer complicated ones. Small circular loops were hard to grip; perforated edges caused paper cuts; plastic covers were frustrating.
change: Loops on the outer tape, inner box, quick-start guide and cable wrap; loops made oval after a tester without fingers on one hand struggled with circles; hinged inner box; front-open pulp tray; no twist ties or plastic; box adjusted so the controller's big buttons don't get pressed in transit.
outcome: Testers reported the box was easy to open. Microsoft described it as its first packaging designed specifically for accessibility and said it was discussing applying the lessons to future products. No metric reported.
attribution: Direct: Microsoft names specific features that came from specific participant feedback.
caveats: First-party feature story; no quantitative outcome. Small number of testers. Promotional context around a product launch.

sources.title: How gamers with disabilities helped design the new Xbox Adaptive Controller's elegantly accessible packaging

title: Duolingo dropped the word 'test' after interviews in Japan and doubled placement tests
summary: Duolingo noticed Japanese learners with prior English were skipping the placement test and quitting from boredom. Interviews revealed the word 'test' itself made people anxious. Rewording it to 'check your English level' doubled placement tests taken, raised retention, and was rolled out globally.
problem: New Japanese learners who already knew some English started at the beginning, found the lessons too easy, and left.
research: Local market research in Japan combining learner data analysis with on-the-ground user research including learner interviews (published 2021).
insight: Learners avoided the placement test because of the word: one said, "The word 'test' scares me." They weren't uninterested in skipping ahead; the framing deterred them.
change: Reworded 'take a placement test' to 'check your English level', tested as an experiment in Japan, then run globally.
outcome: The change doubled placement tests taken and increased retention in Japan. Run globally, it improved placement completion and retention across markets (no exact figures given for retention or the global result).
attribution: Direct: the wording change came from the interview finding and was evaluated as an experiment.
caveats: Duolingo's own blog. Retention lift not quantified. The post calls it an experiment but doesn't describe the design or sample. Primarily an education/learning app; may overlap with the education slice.

sources.title: Lessons from Asia: Turning local research into global experiments

title: Field research in India showed people fear data costs, so YouTube Go shows them
summary: YouTube's research team heard from Indian users in 2014 that YouTube's data use was mysterious and could drain a prepaid pack. Two years of field research in India, Nigeria and Indonesia shaped a separate app, YouTube Go, built around showing data cost, previewing before watching, and offline sharing. Participants also killed one of the team's early concepts.
problem: In markets where most people use prepaid mobile data, YouTube was seen as an expensive, unpredictable data drain, limiting use.
research: Google's YouTube research and design team ran interviews and in-field observation in India, Nigeria and Indonesia (plus user stories from Brazil), watched how people searched for and watched videos, tested prototype concepts, and ran beta tests over roughly two years starting in 2014.
insight: People budget data carefully and avoid anything with unknown cost; they 'peek' at videos before committing; they share videos offline via SD cards and sideloading; they download ahead for offline times; and they want locally relevant content. Participants rejected a low-res keyframes-plus-audio concept because they still wanted good video quality.
change: Built YouTube Go with data cost on every video in the feed, a preview showing keyframes and file size, a choice of quality levels with sizes (e.g. 2MB / 5MB / 12MB), offline peer-to-peer sharing, offline as a normal state, and local trending content. Dropped the keyframe-plus-audio concept.
outcome: No metric published. The research defined the product and killed an early concept; the app launched in India and other markets in 2017.
attribution: Direct: Google ties each core feature to a research finding.
caveats: First-party design story with no sample size or outcome metrics. YouTube Go was later discontinued (2022) in favor of the main app, so its long-term success is unclear.

sources.title: Making YouTube Go

title: Fortnite playtests got 80–90% of players using a mechanic they'd been missing
summary: In early Fortnite playtests, many players either missed the 'weak point' that speeds up resource harvesting or thought it was just a targeting aid. Designers changed its color and placement and turned it into an early unlockable skill. Afterward, 80–90% of playtesters used it.
problem: Harvesting resources felt grindy, and a mechanic meant to speed it up (hitting a weak point) was being ignored or misunderstood.
research: Playtests run by Epic's UX team (led by Celia Hodent) during Fortnite's early development, with video of players; described in a 2018 talk at DigiPen.
insight: Players didn't understand what the weak-point indicator was for. Many treated it as a generic aiming aid or didn't notice it at all. Separately, playtests showed testers spending 10–15 minutes trying to interact with purely decorative objects that looked like objectives.
change: Adjusted the weak point's color and placement, and made it an early unlockable skill in the skill tree rather than something present from the start, so players noticed and valued it.
outcome: After the change, "80 to 90 percent of people finally used the weak points in our playtests," per Hodent. No pre-change percentage given.
attribution: Direct: the change was made in response to playtest observations and re-checked in playtests.
caveats: No baseline number or sample size. Playtest behavior, not live-game data. Account from a university news write-up of a talk. Pre-battle-royale Fortnite (Save the World).

sources.title: Dr. Celia Hodent brings UX insight from Fortnite to DigiPen

title: 1,000 hours on job sites gave the 2021 Ford F-150 a fold-away shifter and sleep seats
summary: For the 2021 F-150, Ford researchers spent over 1,000 hours with people who use trucks as work tools, from ranchers to construction crews. They found owners eat, work and even sleep in their cabs, and still want a real gear lever. That led to a stow-away shifter, a fold-out work surface, near-flat seats and a tailgate workbench.
problem: Ford needed to know how professional owners actually use the cab and bed of a full-size pickup to decide the next F-150's interior and features.
research: Ethnographic field research: Ford researchers documented 'a day in the life' of truck owners across the US, including cattle ranches and construction sites. More than 1,000 hours on site, 18,000+ photos and 600+ videos. Presented by F-150 chief designer Ehab Kaoud in 2021.
insight: Many owners prefer a traditional gear lever over dials or buttons; they eat lunch and do paperwork in the cab like a mobile office; some nap or sleep overnight in the cab at job sites; and the bed is used as a work surface.
change: A physical shift lever that folds away to free console space; an available fold-out work surface big enough for a laptop; Max Recline near-flat seats; an available tailgate workbench with tablet holder and clamping points.
outcome: No metric reported. The research shaped specific interior and tailgate features in the 2021 F-150.
attribution: Trade-press article paraphrasing Ford's chief designer, who links each feature to field findings.
caveats: No sales or satisfaction data tied to the features. Secondary account of a conference presentation, with no direct quotes. Number of participants not stated.

sources.title: Consumers' Voices Echo in Design of 2021 Ford F-150

title: Lyft found 10% of rides were booked for someone else and built a flow for it
summary: Lyft's data showed pickup locations often didn't match the requester's GPS, and a follow-up survey and research confirmed about 10% of rides were for someone else. Those rides had more cancellations, longer pickups and more driver calls. Lyft built a dedicated 'ride for others' experience and cut its notifications after testing.
problem: People ordering rides for others had to relay details by screenshot, riders sometimes used the requester's name for fear of being declined, and these rides caused cancellations, slower pickups and calls from drivers.
research: Data analysis with data scientists (mismatches between pickup and GPS location), a survey suggested by the researcher to confirm the use case, then employee beta, user testing and observation, and review of beta feedback. About 10 months of work, described in 2020.
insight: Around 10% of rides were for someone else, a large hidden use case, and identity confusion between requester, rider and driver was the main pain point.
change: Built a flow to request a ride for another person with the rider's own details. Testing showed an early design sent about 30 notifications to requester and rider; the team cut these to key moments.
outcome: No post-launch metrics reported. Research sized the opportunity and drove the decision to build the feature and to trim its notifications.
attribution: The designer describes the research and data as the basis for prioritizing the feature and for the notification changes.
caveats: No outcome numbers despite baseline problems (cancellations, pickup time) being named. Interview with the designer in Lyft's own 'Behind the Design' series, republished by UX Magazine.

sources.title: Behind the Design: Building a seamless experience to request a ride for others
sources.publisher: UX Magazine (Lyft Behind the Design series)

title: Waymo rider research led to clearer route and drop-off messaging in driverless cars
summary: With no human driver to ask, Waymo riders could be confused when the car took an unexpected route or stopped somewhere unexpected at the end of a trip. Waymo's UX researchers rode along with riders, interviewed them and ran surveys. The service added in-app and in-car messages explaining route differences and setting clearer pull-over expectations.
problem: In a fully driverless ride-hail service, riders can't ask a driver why the car is going a certain way or where exactly it will stop, which undermines trust and comfort.
research: Waymo's UX research team (quoted: senior UX researcher Naomi Guthrie) used ride-alongs with riders, phone and in-person interviews, surveys and questionnaires, and analysis of in-app ride ratings, working with design, engineering, product and operations. Riders in the Phoenix East Valley; described in 2020.
insight: Riders wanted to understand the car's choices, especially when a route differed from what they expected and where the car would pull over at the destination.
change: Added messaging in the Waymo app and on the in-car screen to explain when a route may differ from what a rider expects, and more specific expectations about where the car will pull over at the end of a trip.
outcome: No metric reported. Waymo lists these as changes deployed based on rider feedback.
attribution: Waymo explicitly names these changes as resulting from rider feedback gathered through its research program.
caveats: First-party blog with no numbers, sample sizes or before/after data. Changes described are modest. Promotional context around opening the driverless service to the public.

sources.title: How rider feedback shapes Waymo's fully autonomous ride-hailing service

title: Consulting disabled players gave The Last of Us Part II 60+ accessibility options
company: Naughty Dog / Sony Interactive Entertainment (The Last of Us Part II)
summary: Naughty Dog worked with disabled consultants and playtesters while building The Last of Us Part II. They learned that vision accessibility is a wide spectrum and that players wanted fine-grained control rather than presets. The game shipped with over 60 customizable options, including full text-to-speech and audio cues that let blind players finish it.
problem: Action games routinely lock out players with vision, hearing and motor impairments, and a single 'accessibility mode' can't meet very different needs.
research: During development, Naughty Dog consulted gamers with disabilities, including Steve Saylor (who has a vision impairment), plus other unnamed consultants and playtesters, and experimented with options based on their feedback. Accessibility planned in from the start, per lead designers Emilia Schatz and Matthew Gallant. Released 2020.
insight: Vision accessibility is 'a huge spectrum', so no single setting works. Players didn't fully trust developers to configure things for them and wanted granular control over each option.
change: Shipped over 60 individually customizable options for vision, hearing and motor impairments, including text-to-speech for all on-screen text, a high-contrast mode, an enhanced listening 'sonar' mode, audio cues for navigation and combat, and toggles replacing holds and rapid presses.
outcome: No usage metrics published. Disabled players and advocacy groups widely praised the game; Saylor said, "Now everything is there. And it works."
attribution: Developers describe the option design as shaped by consulting and playtesting with disabled players; NPR reports the options came 'after a lot of experimenting and consulting'.
caveats: No quantitative outcome. Account is journalism quoting the developers and a consultant. The exact count of options varies by source ('around 60', 'over 60').

sources.title: 'The Last Of Us Part II' Presents An Accessible Apocalypse

title: Instagram's like-count research turned a planned removal into a user choice
summary: Instagram set out to make like counts private to reduce pressure on posting. After testing hidden likes with some users since 2019 and hearing from users and experts, it found hidden counts helped some people and annoyed others. Instead of removing like counts for everyone, it made hiding them an option in 2021.
problem: Instagram wanted to know whether hiding public like counts would reduce social pressure on posting, and whether to remove them for everyone.
research: Tests hiding like counts for groups of users starting in 2019, followed by a 2021 test letting users choose, plus feedback from users and outside experts. Instagram did not publish sample sizes or methods.
insight: Not seeing like counts was beneficial for some people and annoying to others, who use likes to see what's trending or popular.
change: Rather than removing like counts globally, Instagram and Facebook let people choose to hide like counts on posts in their feed and on their own posts (May 2021).
outcome: No metric reported. The research changed the decision from a blanket removal to an optional setting.
attribution: Instagram attributes the opt-in approach to what it heard during testing from people and experts.
caveats: Primarily product testing plus feedback; Instagram has not published the research. Critics noted the outcome also preserved engagement metrics advertisers value. No well-being outcome data shared.

sources.title: Giving People More Control on Instagram and Facebook
Instagram's new test lets you choose if you want to hide 'Likes,' Facebook test to follow

title: Blind beta testers shaped Be My AI's safety limits and human fallback
summary: Be My Eyes piloted an AI image-description assistant built on GPT-4V with nearly 200 blind and low-vision testers, growing to 16,000. Testers surfaced confident hallucinations and strongly asked for descriptions of people's faces. The result was explicit warnings against safety-critical use, a one-tap route to a human volunteer, and work to describe people without identifying them by name.
problem: Before launching an AI that describes the visual world to blind users, the team needed to know where it could fail them and how to deploy it responsibly.
research: A pilot from March to early August 2023 with nearly 200 blind and low-vision beta testers, expanding to 16,000 by September 2023 (averaging 25,000 descriptions a day), with an ongoing feedback channel to Be My Eyes leadership.
insight: The model could make basic errors with 'misleading matter-of-fact confidence' (one tester: it 'very confidently told me there was an item on a menu that was in fact not there'). Testers repeatedly said they wanted to know the facial and visible characteristics of people around them, information sighted people get at a glance.
change: Be My Eyes warns users not to rely on the AI for safety or health tasks (prescriptions, allergens, crossing streets) or as a replacement for a cane or guide dog; added an option to leave the AI and connect immediately to a human volunteer; and is designing ways to describe features of people without identifying them by name.
outcome: OpenAI reports that hallucinations and errors noticeably fell in frequency and severity over the beta, and testers noticed better text recognition and richer descriptions. No figures given.
attribution: The system card ties the warnings, fallback and face-description work directly to issues raised by beta testers.
caveats: Beta testing and feedback rather than a structured study; no metrics. Source is OpenAI's own system card, written as part of a launch. Improvements in hallucination may be due to model work rather than the research itself.

sources.title: GPT-4V(ision) System Card

title: Testing with blind users made Pixel's Guided Frame coach in real time and auto-capture
summary: Google set out to help blind and low-vision people take selfies on Pixel phones. A small study with three blind Googlers showed the team was solving the wrong problem, and prototype testing with blind and low-vision volunteers reshaped the feature around real-time audio and haptic guidance and automatic capture. Home testing also revealed demand for group photos.
problem: Taking a well-framed selfie is hard without sight, and the team's first idea focused on helping users find the front camera.
research: Sighted team members first tried eyes-closed selfies; then a preliminary study with three blind Googlers; then iterative prototype testing with blind and low-vision volunteers (including Google's Central Accessibility team, blind and low-vision Googlers, and the Vista Center for the Blind and Visually Impaired), including home testing. Launched with Pixel 7 in 2022.
insight: Users needed live guidance while framing, not just the camera's location. Blind and low-vision users valued automatic capture (not having to find the shutter), even though sighted users generally dislike it. Users also wanted it for group photos.
change: Built voice instructions telling users whether they are left, right or centered; combined audio cues, haptics and high-contrast visuals; made the camera capture automatically once the face is centered; extended support to group photos.
outcome: No metric reported. Testing changed the core interaction and scope of the feature.
attribution: Google states the early study showed the team had been focused on the wrong solution, and that testing feedback set the final mix of cues and auto-capture.
caveats: Small, partly internal sample (three blind Googlers in the first study); first-party blog with no outcome data.

sources.title: How we tested Guided Frame and Real Tone on Pixel

title: Remote playtests helped Snake.io lift tutorial completions 40%
summary: After acquiring the mobile game Snake.io, Kooapps used PlaytestCloud's remote playtests, both single-session and longitudinal, to guide a series of changes to art style, scoring visibility and reward progression. The vendor reports tutorial completions up 40% and Day 1 and Day 3 retention up 10%.
problem: Kooapps needed to improve Day 1 retention and grow daily active users for Snake.io, and adapt it for a younger audience.
research: Iterative remote playtests via PlaytestCloud: single-session tests for first impressions and longitudinal tests for longer-term play. Number of players and rounds not stated.
insight: The vendor does not detail specific findings; the playtests pointed to the art style, how visible scores were, and reward progression as areas to improve.
change: Refreshed the art style, added character skins, made scores and leaderboards more visible, added reward progression, and added live events and boss modes.
outcome: Day 1 and Day 3 retention up 10%; tutorial completions up 40%; rewarded-video ad conversions up 10%. Art-style changes alone were credited with a 5% Day 1 retention lift.
attribution: The vendor credits the playtest-driven changes, but doesn't explain how the lifts were measured or separate them from other factors.
caveats: Vendor marketing about its own client. No method for the metrics, no dates, no sample sizes, no control. Several changes shipped together.

sources.title: Kooapps case study

title: Emotion research and seven-country testing picked Facebook's five Reactions
summary: To give people more ways to respond than 'Like', Facebook worked with UC Berkeley psychologist Dacher Keltner, whose lab had already tested which emotion illustrations people could reliably recognize. Keltner's team proposed 43 ideas; Facebook narrowed them and tested in seven countries before launch, dropping a planned 'Yay' reaction because it wasn't used in some countries.
problem: 'Like' felt wrong for sad or upsetting posts, but Facebook needed a small set of reactions that would be instantly understood across cultures and 70+ languages.
research: Keltner's lab had earlier shown about 40 emotion illustrations to dozens to hundreds of people to check recognition (for Messenger stickers). For Reactions, his team proposed 43 ideas about a year before launch. Facebook then tested candidate reactions in seven countries, including Ireland and Spain, before the 2016 global launch.
insight: Each reaction had to be 'extremely easily recognizable' everywhere; some candidates, like 'Yay', didn't get used in some countries.
change: Launched five reactions alongside Like (Love, Haha, Wow, Sad, Angry), dropped 'Yay', and kept the same set and near-identical translations worldwide.
outcome: No usage or outcome numbers in the source. Research shaped which reactions shipped and killed one.
attribution: The article links the chosen set to Keltner's recognition research and the multi-country tests, and the dropped 'Yay' directly to test results.
caveats: Journalism based on interviews with Facebook and Keltner; methods of the country tests aren't described. No outcome data. 2016.

sources.title: Facebook's Long, Psychological Journey To Reactions

title: British Gas bill redesign cut query calls by 3,000 a week
summary: British Gas wanted fewer billing query calls and happier customers. Research with customers and service providers showed bills were overloaded and didn't answer the questions people actually had. The simplified bill launched in 2012 and calls fell by about 10%.
problem: UK energy bills were widely criticised as complicated and opaque. British Gas, serving around 10 million customers, received a large volume of query calls about its bills.
research: Lippincott ran research with customers and with service providers (the people handling bill queries). Existing research and input from government regulators and consumer watchdogs fed into the same phase. Participant numbers are not given.
insight: Customers come to a bill with five questions: what do I owe, how do I pay, how can I save, how can I control it, and can you help me. Around 30% of the information printed on the bill was not needed.
change: The bill was cut down to what was needed, jargon was removed, it was structured around those key questions, and customers were pointed to one central phone number. The framing shifted from a demand for money to a way to save money.
outcome: After launch (August 2012), the case study reports a reduction of 3,000 calls per week (10%), a saving of more than £750,000 to the organisation, and 17% of customers finding the information clearer. The EU later cited the bill as best practice.
attribution: Moderate. The research findings map directly onto the new bill structure, and the call reduction is measured after implementation, but other factors (pricing news, seasonality) are not controlled for.
caveats: Short case study reproduced with the agency's permission on an EU service-design project site; reads as promotional. No method for the call measurement, no participant numbers, and the savings period (per year?) is not stated. Old (2012).

sources.title: Redesigning the British Gas billing experience (case study)
sources.publisher: SHAPE Better Services (reproduced with permission of British Gas and Lippincott)

title: Sage's research-led site changes lifted Intacct page conversion
summary: Sage's digital experience team used surveys, usability studies and benchmark scores to find where prospects struggled on sage.com. Each change was framed as a hypothesis tied to a customer insight and then run as an experiment. The vendor reports conversion gains in several markets, including an average 22% rise on Intacct pages.
problem: Product pages on sage.com were long and overwhelming, navigation made it hard to find the right product, and product benefits were unclear, which the team believed was holding back conversion.
research: Ongoing user surveys and remote studies on the UserTesting platform, analysis of customer feedback, click paths and task completion rates, and QXscore benchmarking of sage.com alongside NPS and brand metrics. Changes were written as 'IF variable THEN outcome DUE TO customer insight' hypotheses. Dates and sample sizes are not given (story appears to date from around 2024).
insight: Prospects were overwhelmed by page length, could not easily find relevant solutions, and did not understand product benefits.
change: Added step-by-step product tours for Sage Intacct, simplified navigation with filters on the All Products page, added support badges and sections, used more dynamic hero visuals, and shortened product pages with clearer calls to action.
outcome: Intacct product tour: conversion up 12% (UK), 7% (US) and 47% (AU), described as a 22% average increase. Support information: form completions up 31% (UK). Hero visuals: trial signups up 10% (UK), 36% (South Africa), 29% (Ireland). Simplified product pages: conversion up 15% (UK), 8% (US). QXscore up an average of 6 points across UK Intacct, Accounting and Payroll pages.
attribution: Partial. The hypothesis framework explicitly ties each change to a customer insight, and the page calls the results 'targeted experiments', but the link between specific studies and specific changes is only stated for the product tour.
caveats: Vendor (UserTesting) customer story. No description of test design, sample sizes, durations or significance, so rated 'reported' even though experiments are mentioned. Many market-level results may include cherry-picking (170 experiments were run). Undated.

sources.title: Sage customer story

title: ComEd rebuilt its electricity bill around what customers said mattered
summary: ComEd's customer satisfaction hit a historic low in 2012, and survey analysis pointed to the bill as the most influential touchpoint. The utility gathered customer input through focus groups, surveys and an online 'Bill Builder', tested shortlisted designs with customers, and launched a new bill in 2014. ComEd and its survey vendor credit it with an industry-leading rise in satisfaction.
problem: ComEd ranked lowest among large Midwest electric utilities on J.D. Power's customer satisfaction index, in the bottom quartile on 39 of 40 drivers. Customers were confused about pricing and did not realise most charges on the bill were for power supply rather than ComEd's delivery.
research: A survey driver analysis identified the billing statement as the most critical touchpoint. From May 2013, ComEd collected customer input via focus groups, surveys, Facebook and an online 'Bill Builder' tool. Three finalist designs (from a crowdsourced competition with more than 280 entries) went back to customers for feedback, heat-map survey questions compared existing and proposed designs, and the final bill was tested with residential customers. Sample sizes are not published.
insight: Customers cared most about the bill summary and amount due, then usage and meter information, and wanted to understand supply charges separately from delivery charges.
change: The new bill, launched March 2014, ordered information by importance, put summarised usage and charges on the front, clearly separated supply from delivery charges, colour-coded sections and moved contact details and messages to the back. It went to nearly 4 million households in under a year.
outcome: Qualtrics' customer story reports an 'industry-leading rise in customer satisfaction' and a J.D. Power award. No satisfaction scores, call volumes or other figures are given.
attribution: Weak to moderate. The research clearly shaped the bill, but the satisfaction rise is reported at company level and other ComEd initiatives over the same period likely contributed.
caveats: Outcome claim comes from the survey vendor's customer story, with no numbers or method. The independent press coverage (2014) documents the research process but reports no results. Crowdsourced design competition was part of the process, not just research.

sources.title: ComEd customer story
ComEd debuts customer bill with crowdsourced redesign

title: GitLab settings redesign raised first-click success from 34% to 97% on a key task
summary: Users told GitLab its group settings were hard to find after they were folded into collapsible sections with vague labels. The team reorganised the page around the settings most people look for and then measured the old and new versions with click tests involving more than 600 participants. Success rates rose sharply on two of three tasks, though time on task did not improve.
problem: After group and project settings were moved into expandable sections, users reported that they couldn't find settings. Section labels were not descriptive, so people had to open sections and guess.
research: User reports gathered in a public discovery issue shaped the redesign. After the group settings pilot shipped (GitLab 11.5), the designer ran two unmoderated first-click tests on UsabilityHub, one per version: 389 participants saw the original and 266 the redesign, recruited via Twitter and GitLab's research mailing list. Each had three 'where would you click to...' tasks plus 1-5 ratings of ease and confidence. Published March 2019.
insight: A small share of settings (roughly the 20% most people look for) accounted for most visits, and vague section labels were the main reason people guessed wrong.
change: The most-used settings were given their own prominent section, vague labels were replaced with descriptive ones, whole section titles became clickable, and some content was moved.
outcome: First-click success: task 1 went from 77% to 78%, task 2 from 34% to 97%, task 3 from 49% to 92%. Mean confidence rose on tasks 1 and 2 (3.6 to 4.1, 3.2 to 4.1) but dipped on task 3 (3.9 to 3.7). Time to click got worse on tasks 1 and 3 and better on task 2, so the team's assumption about speed was not validated.
attribution: Direct. The redesign came from user-reported problems, and the outcome is measured by comparing the two designs on identical tasks.
caveats: Separate unmoderated tests with unequal, self-selected samples (GitLab followers), not a randomized live A/B test. Measures findability in a click test, not real-world support load or usage. Mixed results on time and on task 3 difficulty. Only the group settings page was tested.

sources.title: Quantifying UX: validating the redesign of GitLab's settings pages

title: GitLab research steered it away from organising navigation by DevOps stage
summary: GitLab considered reorganising its product navigation around its DevOps lifecycle stages, matching how the company described itself. A series of research studies suggested this would make features harder to find, because stage names like 'Manage' and 'Create' don't tell users what is inside. The team did not pursue that structure.
problem: As GitLab grew, its navigation had to hold more and more features. Internally, the company organised itself around DevOps stages, and there was interest in making the UI follow the same structure.
research: A series of research studies on whether stage-based navigation would work, building on earlier usability testing rounds that informed the 2017 navigation redesign. The post does not give methods or participant counts for the stage studies. Reported July 2019.
insight: Stage-based sub-navigation would add steps, and stage names are not self-explanatory, especially to people unfamiliar with GitLab's DevOps vocabulary. Context and discoverability were the recurring problems.
change: GitLab kept its existing global/contextual navigation model with incremental changes, rather than restructuring it around DevOps stages, and planned further interviews and journey mapping.
outcome: In the post's words, findings from the studies 'cautioned us against moving in that direction'. No metric is reported.
attribution: Stated directly by GitLab's UX researcher, though the post doesn't describe the studies in detail.
caveats: Light on method detail. The post describes ongoing work, so the decision may have been revisited later. No measure of what was avoided.

sources.title: Navigation: state of play

title: Google survey of 10,000 developers reshaped its internal infrastructure tooling strategy
summary: Google's internal infrastructure tools had grown into hundreds of separately built, inconsistent UIs. A survey of 10,000 Googlers, follow-up interviews and service blueprinting showed debugging was the biggest pain point and won executive support for consolidation. Research also led the team to extend an existing console instead of building a new bespoke one.
problem: Google has over 1,000 internal tools built by different teams. Developers found infrastructure tools hard to discover, inconsistent, hard to onboard to and slow to troubleshoot, which cost engineering time.
research: In November 2021 the team surveyed 10,000 randomly selected Googlers (1,300 responded, 749 gave open-ended feedback). They followed up with 60-minute semi-structured interviews with 23 users, a cross-functional story-mapping workshop, critical-user-journey validation interviews, a service blueprint, logs analysis, and three rounds of RITE (rapid iterative testing) on redesigns and a pipeline prototype.
insight: Debuggability was the biggest problem, making up 67% of open-ended feedback: the information existed but was scattered across dashboards and UIs. Performance and reliability made up another 19%. Stakeholder interviews also showed that past measurement dashboards were usually abandoned, so the team chose one success metric (engineer capacity saved) instead.
change: The team built a vision for a unified console and used it to secure executive buy-in. After evaluating options, they chose to extend an existing infrastructure console (Sigma) rather than build a bespoke console modelled on Google Cloud's, shipped a readability redesign of a job page, and designed a 'Needs Attention' pipeline page tested through three RITE rounds.
outcome: The paper reports executive buy-in and incremental shipped improvements. Projected savings were estimated at 69 (conservative), 208 (moderate) or 1,663 (aggressive) full-time engineers' worth of capacity per year, but these are forecasts, not measured results. The pipeline MVP was still to be released at the time of writing.
attribution: Direct for the decisions: the authors state the survey and interviews defined the problem and that the evaluation drove the choice to extend Sigma. No measured outcome yet.
caveats: Short CHI 2025 workshop submission written by the team itself. Savings figures are internal estimates. The paper notes Gemini was used to edit parts of the text. The redesign's effect on time-to-find information is described qualitatively.

sources.title: From 600 Tools to 1 Console: A UX-Driven Transformation

title: EE's prototype testing raised chatbot containment by 75% and trimmed calls 2.4%
summary: EE's research team found that its chatbot, Aimee, was swamped with roaming questions it could not answer, pushing most of them to phone advisers. Iterative prototype testing with current, prospective and competitors' customers shaped a new chatbot version, a roaming calculator and a reorganised app navigation. The vendor reports a 75% rise in chatbot containment and a 2.4% drop in contact-centre calls.
problem: Aimee, EE's chatbot, resolved only 16% of roaming questions directly; the rest became calls to advisers. Separately, the app homepage was crowded and common account actions were hard to find.
research: Embedded researchers and designers ran iterative remote tests of sketches and prototypes with existing EE customers, prospective customers and people using competitors' products, via the UserTesting platform. For roaming, the team modelled likely trips and package costs and tested new prototypes with participants. Sample sizes and dates are not given (story appears to date from around 2024).
insight: Customers' roaming questions were too varied for the old bot, and a dedicated 'Manage' area would reduce homepage cognitive load and make account tasks easier to find.
change: Launched a new version of Aimee that answered roaming questions more accurately, added a roaming calculator, added a 'Manage' area to app navigation, and aligned the information architecture across app and web and logged-in and logged-out states.
outcome: Reported: 75% increase in chatbot containment, 2.4% decrease in calls to the contact centre, 50% more click-through from the roaming calculator, 50% uplift in traffic to broadband pages, and 'Manage' became the most popular hub destination in the app within its first month.
attribution: Moderate. The research finding (16% roaming resolution) leads directly to the chatbot change, but outcomes are reported without method, baseline period or control, and several changes shipped together.
caveats: Vendor (UserTesting) customer story. No dates, sample sizes or measurement method. The 2.4% call reduction is small and could reflect other factors. Several other gains are claimed without figures.

sources.title: EE (BT Group) customer story

title: Monzo's gambling block, shaped by affected customers, used by ~100,000 people in 10 months
summary: Monzo customers on its community forum asked for a way to block their own gambling spending. Monzo built a card-level gambling block shaped by that feedback and tested with people who had requested it, deliberately making it harder to turn off than on. A 2023 update, developed with GamCare and people with lived experience of gambling harm, added longer cooldowns and personal notes.
problem: Some customers experiencing gambling harm wanted their bank to help them stop impulsive gambling spending, and there was no self-exclusion tool at the bank level.
research: In 2018 Monzo drew on feedback and experiences shared on its community forum and tested the feature with a few people who had requested it. For the 2023 improvements it worked with the charity GamCare, customers, industry experts and people with first-hand experience of gambling harm, and benchmarked itself against GamCare's recommendations for banks. Methods and sample sizes are not described.
insight: Gambling is often impulsive, so a block that can be lifted instantly offers little protection; people who turn it on want friction that gives them time to reconsider.
change: The 2018 block required contacting support and then waiting 48 hours before it could be switched off. In 2023 Monzo added cooldown options of up to a year, a personal note shown when a cooldown starts and ends, and routing to specialist support teams for customers who had disclosed gambling harm.
outcome: Monzo's 2023 post says close to 100,000 people used the block in the previous 10 months, more than 200,000 attempted gambling transactions were blocked, and its compliance with GamCare's recommendations rose from 45% to 87%. No data on whether users' gambling harm fell.
attribution: Moderate for the design (Monzo says customer feedback shaped how the block was built); weak for the outcome, which is adoption rather than an effect of research-driven design choices.
caveats: Research is informal (forum feedback, small testing group) and not described in detail. Outcome figures are Monzo's own and measure uptake and blocked transactions, not reduced harm. Blocked attempts may include repeated attempts by the same people.

sources.title: How to block gambling spending from your Monzo account
We've improved our gambling block

title: Credit Sesame's research-tested iOS relaunch lifted completed registrations 31.7%
summary: Credit Sesame, a US credit and financial wellness platform, redesigned its iOS app to improve trust, engagement and conversion. Its researchers ran unmoderated usability tests, think-alouds, comparative studies and surveys across onboarding, navigation and messaging. Comparing the months before and after the July 2023 release, completed registrations rose 31.7% and the app's rating went from 3.19 to 4.11.
problem: The iOS app needed to do better on engagement, trust and conversion, particularly through onboarding and account creation.
research: Unmoderated usability tests, think-aloud sessions, comparative studies and surveys run on the UserTesting platform, covering onboarding and account creation, navigation and decisions about credit products, clarity and emotional tone of messaging, and trust signals. Sample sizes are not given. The redesigned app shipped on 13 July 2023 (versions 6.0.0 and 6.0.1).
insight: The story names the areas studied (onboarding, navigation, messaging, trust indicators) but does not list specific findings.
change: A redesigned and relaunched iOS app. Specific design changes are not described.
outcome: Before/after comparison: completed registrations +31.7%, new users +18.4%, subscriptions +14.3%, credit card click-applies +1.6%, email open rate +18.3%. Net Fan Score 30 to 54, 'love for experience' score 28% to 70%, in-app rating 3.19 to 4.11.
attribution: Moderate. The research fed the redesign, but outcomes compare the whole release before and after, and the source itself says it does not isolate the redesign's effect from other factors.
caveats: Vendor (UserTesting) customer story. No sample sizes, no specific findings or changes, and no control group. The page notes results come from the months around release and may not reflect later updates. Experience scores are the vendor's own metrics.

sources.title: Credit Sesame customer story

title: Banco Sabadell made a usability score a launch gate and reports 50% faster delivery
summary: Spanish bank Banco Sabadell requires every digital experience to pass customer testing and reach a minimum benchmark score before it goes to engineering and launch. It ran more than 500 tests in a year, including over 40 on online account opening. The vendor reports a 50% increase in speed to market, and more than half of new customers now open accounts online.
problem: The bank was moving key journeys, such as account opening, from branches to digital channels and needed a consistent way to decide whether designs were ready to build and ship.
research: More than 500 remote tests in one year with prospective and existing customers on the UserTesting platform, covering account creation, sign-in, bill payment, loan simulation, insurance and navigation. Designers compared options with customers, tracked drop-offs and clicks, and scored each experience with QXscore (a vendor usability-and-enjoyment benchmark). Over 40 tests went into online account signup. Roughly 2023.
insight: Comparative testing of design options showed which version customers could complete and preferred, letting teams settle choices with evidence rather than opinion.
change: A minimum QXscore of 85 became mandatory before any digital experience can go live; scores are logged in Jira and project managers use them to decide whether work moves to the next phase. Online account opening was built and refined through repeated testing.
outcome: Reported: 50% increase in the speed of bringing projects to market (also described as research project speed up 50%), and account opening moved from branch-only a year earlier to more than half of new customers opening online.
attribution: Weak to moderate. The speed claim is about the research process itself, and the shift to online account opening also reflects the bank's decision to offer it online at all.
caveats: Vendor (UserTesting) customer story about its own proprietary metric. No baseline or method for the 50% figure. Undated. The online-signup share is not a research effect on its own.

sources.title: Banco Sabadell customer story

title: Everypaw pet insurance tested its TV ad with owners; quote starts after airings rose 85%
summary: Everypaw, a UK pet insurer with about 5% market share, was producing its first 30-second TV ad and the internal team was split on key choices. It tested ad variants with UK pet owners considering insurance, which settled the music, the value propositions to lead with and the ending screen. The vendor reports an 85% rise in people starting a quote within five minutes of airings, versus the previous year's campaign.
problem: The team needed to choose between creative options for a costly TV campaign, with executives split (for example 50/50 on the music) and worries that the CGI and ending screen would distract viewers.
research: Remote tests on the UserTesting panel with women aged 25-55 in the UK who own pets and were considering pet insurance. Ad clips were shown in A/B variants to compare background music, a voiceover with three value propositions, and an ending screen with a call to action. Participant numbers are not given (story appears to date from around 2024).
insight: Viewers strongly preferred one song, enjoyed the CGI rather than being distracted, valued 24/7 access to vets and experts far more than the free dog activity tracker, and liked the ending screen, with most saying they would visit the site on mobile.
change: The ad was adjusted before airing based on participant feedback, including the music choice and which value propositions to emphasise.
outcome: An 85% increase in engagement versus the previous year's campaign, where engagement means visiting the website within five minutes of the ad airing and starting a quote. The story also claims increased market share, with no figure.
attribution: Weak. Testing shaped creative choices, but the comparison is with a different, earlier campaign, so media spend, timing and the creative concept itself all differ.
caveats: Vendor (UserTesting) customer story. Marketing research on an advert, not product UX. Year-on-year comparison with no control. Sample size unknown. The story also loosely calls the result 'twice the number of people', which does not match 85%.

sources.title: Everypaw (Cardif Pinnacle) customer story

title: Purefy's borrower interviews led to a landing-page fix that lifted conversion 36%
summary: Student loan refinancing startup Purefy interviewed 25 borrowers and parents to understand how they research refinancing and how they reacted to its website. Within about ten interviews a clear theme emerged: a key landing page tried to say too many things at once. The team simplified the page's messaging and A/B tested it, reporting a 36% lift in conversion.
problem: Purefy wanted to understand hesitant prospects' decision-making and improve its web presence and positioning as a relatively unknown brand.
research: Twenty-five hour-long moderated remote interviews (dscout Live) over about a month in 2021, with borrowers and parents of borrowers interested in refinancing, recruited via video screener questions. Interviews covered how people research refinancing and live reactions to Purefy's site, with UX, design, copy and content staff observing.
insight: A key landing page presented several value propositions at once, so Purefy's message was unclear. Prospects also needed more trust signals and social proof. Three distinct segments emerged: new graduates, experienced refinancers and parents.
change: After a debrief around interview ten, the team made immediate language and sequencing changes, drafted a simplified landing page within a week, and the UX researcher set up an A/B test while interviews were still running. Three personas were created for marketing.
outcome: The CMO is quoted: 'That one change, which we noticed early on, resulted in a 36% lift in conversion.'
attribution: Direct. The tested change came straight from an interview finding, and it was evaluated with an A/B test.
caveats: Vendor (dscout) case study. No baseline conversion, sample size, test duration or significance reported, and the exact variant isn't described. Small startup, single test.

sources.title: Purefy case study

title: Lender's research-led repayment redesign raised autopay activation 25%
summary: An unnamed Bay Area fintech lender worked with consultancy Coforge to understand why borrowers weren't setting up autopay and were falling behind. Generative interviews, surveys and contextual inquiry with different borrower types fed simplified repayment flows that were then usability tested. The consultancy reports a 25% rise in autopay activation and a 50% fall in delinquency.
problem: Too few borrowers were activating autopay, and loan delinquency was a concern.
research: Generative research with user interviews, surveys and contextual inquiries, aimed at personas including debt-burdened borrowers and people with stable incomes; low- and high-fidelity concepts validated through user testing; analytics after launch. Sample sizes and dates are not given.
insight: The source says research uncovered behavioural insights about borrowers' financial stress and repayment behaviour but does not spell them out.
change: Simplified repayment workflows and clearer, more personalised financial interactions, refined after launch using analytics.
outcome: Reported: 25% increase in autopay activation and 50% reduction in loan delinquency rates. Satisfaction and engagement described only as 'improved'.
attribution: Unclear. The consultancy presents the outcome as a result of its research-led redesign but gives no baseline, period or method.
caveats: Vendor (Coforge) success story about an anonymous client. No findings described, no baseline or measurement period. A 50% drop in delinquency is a large claim that could reflect many factors (economy, underwriting, collections policy). Undated. The page is undated; the year field reflects when it was found, not when the work happened.

sources.title: Driving higher autopay adoption with research-led experience redesign

title: Slack's 2020 redesign changed course on several features after a 100-user pilot and benchmark tests
summary: Slack's 2020 interface redesign started as rough internal prototypes aimed at cutting clutter. A months-long co-design pilot with about 100 customers and benchmark tests with people new to Slack reversed or reshaped several planned changes, from hiding member counts to where the compose button sat. A second benchmark found the new design beat or tied the old one on core tasks.
problem: Slack had grown more capable but harder to use, especially for new users. The team wanted a simpler interface but didn't know whether its tidier prototypes were actually more usable.
research: A shared Slack channel pilot with about 100 users from Slack's champion network across dozens of organisations, running for weeks to months with ongoing feedback. Usability benchmarking comparing old and new designs with people who had never used Slack (tasks: send a message, search, find and join channels), repeated after changes, plus similar studies with average Slack users. Participant counts for benchmarks not given. Published March 2020.
insight: Member counts help people 'read the room' in a channel. New users ignored a compose button at the bottom of the sidebar, often tried right-clicking, and missed key features when sections started collapsed. Users preferred familiar search placement over novel layouts.
change: Restored the channel member count the team had planned to hide; made the custom-sections entry point less prominent with an in-product prompt; chose a conventional top-navigation search layout; moved compose to the top of the sidebar; built fuller right-click menus across the app; made collapsible views start open.
outcome: After these changes, the new design 'beat or tied' the existing one on the benchmark tasks, which the authors cite as the basis for confidence in the release. No numbers are given.
attribution: Direct for the design decisions: each change is tied to a specific pilot or benchmark finding. The benchmark result is reported only qualitatively.
caveats: First-party blog post with no sample sizes, task-success figures or post-launch metrics. Pilot participants were Slack champions, who are not typical users. Rated 'decision' because no measured outcome is shared.

sources.title: Designing teamwork: How our customers helped shape the future of Slack

title: Slack moved search back to the top after research showed users couldn't find it
summary: In its 2023 redesign Slack tried moving search into the left-hand navigation to simplify the interface. User research, pilot customer feedback and internal usage data all showed people couldn't find it there. Slack moved search back to the top of the window before wide release.
problem: Slack's navigation was reaching its limits: people on large, busy teams struggled to keep up with basics and to find Slack's growing set of features.
research: Provocative early prototypes discussed with users, user research on search placement, pilot customers using early designs, internal usage data, regular conversations with internal users and pilot customers, and pulse surveys of internal and external users. Methods and sample sizes are not described. Around 2023.
insight: With search in the left-hand navigation, it 'just wasn't findable' for users.
change: Search was moved back to the top of the interface. The authors say other changes were also revisited after pulse surveys and pilot feedback, without naming them.
outcome: A design decision was reversed before launch. No metrics are reported.
attribution: Direct: the authors (Slack's VP of Product Design and a principal PM) state that research, pilot feedback and usage data drove the reversal.
caveats: First-party post with no method detail or numbers. Undated on the page (images suggest 2023). Usage data contributed alongside research, so research was one of several signals.

sources.title: How our biggest redesign yet came to be

title: Xero reworked its new invoicing screens after users said they were slower
summary: Xero launched a new invoicing experience that many small-business users found slower than the old one. Reviewing user feedback and then watching users work through invoices showed extra clicks, broken keyboard navigation and a harder-to-read layout. Xero shipped a set of fixes, began redesigning the page layout and extended the availability of classic invoicing.
problem: After the new invoicing experience launched, users reported it took more clicks and was harder to use than classic invoicing, a core daily task for small businesses.
research: Analysis of user feedback on the new experience, followed by observational sessions sitting beside users as they clicked and tabbed through invoicing screens, and recruitment for a beta programme to test and co-design features. Participant numbers are not given. Reported May 2024, updated November 2024.
insight: The new experience required more clicks, changes to keyboard navigation slowed invoice creation for keyboard-heavy users, and the new layout made the invoice page harder to read and navigate.
change: Deleting a line item went from two clicks to one; Tab in branding and tax fields now selects and moves on; the date field accepts typing immediately; attachments preview in place; single clicks for printing/downloading, creating another invoice, sending receipts and marking as sent; invoice number shown in the browser tab. A redesign of the top half of the create-invoice page was started, and classic invoicing was kept available until 27 February 2025.
outcome: Specific usability fixes shipped and the retirement of classic invoicing was postponed. No metrics are reported.
attribution: Direct for the changes: Xero's Head of Product lists the fixes as responses to what users reported and what researchers observed.
caveats: First-party post responding to customer complaints, so partly reputation management. Research happened after launch, not before. No numbers on how many users were observed or whether the fixes improved speed. The postponement may have had other reasons.

sources.title: How your feedback is helping us improve the new invoicing experience

title: Insure4Retirement doubled quote completion after usability testing moved contact questions later
summary: Insure4Retirement, an online home insurance broker for over-50s, had its quote-and-buy journey usability tested before rebuilding it. Testing showed people disliked giving contact details on the first page but accepted it once they had built their policy, and profiling revealed many users were buying on behalf of older relatives. After the rebuild, the agency reports quote completion rising from about 37% to about 77%.
problem: The broker was rebuilding its online quote-and-buy journey and wanted more visitors to get through to a price.
research: Usability testing of the existing quote-and-buy journey before the build, a user profiling project, a workshop with the broker and its design agency to map wireframes and the question set, and a second usability test of the brochure site after changes. Participant numbers are not given. The work appears to date from around 2016.
insight: Users reacted badly to entering personal contact details on the first page but were much more accepting once they had built their product. An extra core audience emerged: people arranging cover for older relatives or friends. Of 30 recommendations, 15-20 covered problems the team had not expected to matter as much.
change: Contact-detail questions were moved later in the journey, the question set and flow were reworked in a joint workshop, and the brochure site was tweaked after a second round of testing.
outcome: Quote start to quote completion (reaching a price) went from about 37% to about 77%. Overall visitor-to-quote completion went from 6% to over 20% after the brochure site changes. Digital marketing cost per acquisition fell to 'double-digit figures' (no exact numbers). The headline claims a 300% increase without explaining the calculation.
attribution: Moderate. Specific research findings map to specific changes, but the comparison is before/after a full rebuild, judged in January (a peak month), with no control.
caveats: Agency (Experience UX) writing about its own client. Seasonality may inflate the after figures. No sample sizes, dates or exact periods. The '300%' headline figure is unexplained.

sources.title: UX Case Study – Insure4Retirement – Driving a 300% increased conversion rate

title: Figma interviews and data reveal hidden notification bell and missing alerts, reshaping its roadmap
summary: Figma's activity team didn't know where in the notification funnel to focus. A researcher and a data scientist worked in parallel: interviews showed users lived in their email and never visited the file browser where the bell sat, and data showed most users received no notifications at all. The team moved the bell, centred experiments on team-account users, and shipped comment notifications for file editors, not just owners.
problem: Figma wanted people to engage more with notifications, but the activity team couldn't tell whether the weak point was enablement, delivery, viewing or interaction.
research: Over several weeks in 2023, a Figma user researcher ran interviews (including observing workflows) while a data scientist analysed the notification funnel. They split open questions by which method could answer them and held regular joint synthesis sessions.
insight: Interviewees said they relied heavily on email notifications, which clashed with data showing low email engagement. Re-cutting the data by account type explained it: designers on team accounts opened 80% of comment-notification emails, while many other users simply received nothing ('71% of users don't receive any notifications'). Interviews also showed people rarely visited the file browser, so the bell in its top-right corner was 'out of sight and out of mind'. Collaborators who weren't file owners got no comment notifications at all.
change: The bell was moved to a more prominent spot at the upper left of the file browser. The team made team-account users the reference group for notification experiments, and after an experiment released comment notifications for file editors, not only owners.
outcome: The post reports the changes and says the work shaped the half's roadmap and a series of experiments. It gives no metric for the effect of the changes.
attribution: Direct for the decisions: the bell move and the team-account focus are traced to specific interview and data findings. The editor-notification change came partly from the researchers' own experience and was then tested in an experiment, results not shared.
caveats: Figma's own blog, written as a showcase of its research practice. No outcome numbers for the shipped changes. The 80% and 71% figures describe the problem, not the result.

sources.title: How Figma's data science and user research teams weave together insights that count

title: Mozilla's 61-person value study made the case for small-audience Firefox Focus
summary: Mozilla researchers ran a diary study, interviews and workshops with 61 people in six cities to learn how people describe the value they get from Firefox. Leaders had been debating whether to keep investing in Firefox Focus, a privacy browser with a small user base. The research showed Focus is often used alongside another Firefox browser and plays a critical role in some people's workflows, which the team calls its most tangible success.
problem: Mozilla measured success mainly through usage numbers like monthly active users, and collects little data on what people do in the browser. By that yardstick, Firefox Focus looked small, and there was internal discussion about whether to keep spending limited resources on it.
research: In late 2019 and early 2020, Firefox user researchers studied 61 participants in Berlin, Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Taipei and Vancouver in three phases: a three-day diary study, remote interviews, and in-person workshops (including scenario-building and participant 'pitch videos' to Mozilla leaders). Follow-up surveys of thousands of people checked the use-case categories at scale. Leaders and stakeholders took part in the activities.
insight: People's most valued uses of Firefox fell into a stable set of categories, and high usage wasn't always good for them (for example, huge numbers of open tabs felt overwhelming). Firefox Focus, despite its small audience, was often used alongside another Firefox mobile browser for specific jobs and mattered a lot in those workflows.
change: The study gave leadership evidence to look beyond raw usage numbers when judging Firefox Focus, and the use-case categories fed into further mixed-method research and survey work.
outcome: The authors say the most tangible success was highlighting the value of Firefox Focus to leadership teams that had been questioning investment in it. They don't state a formal decision or any metric.
attribution: Moderate. The researchers say their study (along with a colleague's research) showed Focus's value. The post doesn't say what was decided or that the research was the deciding factor.
caveats: Self-reported impact by the researchers who ran the study. Influence on a funding debate, not a measured outcome. 2021 post.

sources.title: Who Gets to Define Success? Listening to Stories of How People Value Firefox to Redefine Metrics

title: Interviews with Firefox Picture-in-Picture users stop Mozilla treating 'habit' as the success metric
summary: Data showed some Firefox users were forming a habit with Picture-in-Picture video. Mozilla interviewed and observed 11 of them to learn why. People used it to take notes, focus, calm down or break up monotonous work, not as a distraction. The team decided not to measure PiP's success by habit formation and instead to support what people already did, adding controls such as volume.
problem: About six months after launch, usage data showed PiP users opened more PiP windows over time. The team didn't know why, and worried the feature might hurt productivity by adding distraction.
research: In 2020, Firefox researchers interviewed 11 people who used Picture-in-Picture and watched them use it in their everyday browsing.
insight: PiP often helped people get tasks done: a student watched lectures while taking notes, others used background video to stay motivated during dull work or to calm down while reading something hard. The team found nothing seriously wrong that would stop habit formation.
change: The team decided not to make 'habit-forming' the measure of PiP's success, and to better support existing uses instead, starting with more controls such as changing the volume. A separate experiment on PiP discoverability was prepared at the same time.
outcome: A change in product strategy and feature priorities. No usage or satisfaction metrics are reported for the changes.
attribution: Direct for the strategy change: the post's 'Our research impact' section ties it to the interviews.
caveats: Small qualitative sample (11 people). Mozilla's own blog. No outcome data.

sources.title: From a Feature to a Habit: Why are People Watching Videos in Picture-in-Picture?

title: Firefox's rewritten security warnings cut stated intent to ignore them by 22–50%
summary: About 3% of Firefox users hit a certificate security warning every day, and the old pages were full of jargon. Mozilla's content and UX team rewrote them using published warning research and its own usability tests, then compared versions in a survey. People shown the new pages were 22–50% less likely to say they'd ignore the warning, and a live comparison found no harm to usage or retention.
problem: Firefox's certificate error pages used vague technical language in a dated design. Mozilla wanted people to understand the risk and avoid unsafe sites, without driving them to switch browsers.
research: Three studies in 2018: an unmoderated remote usability study with eight participants on a first draft of the new pages; a paid-panel survey comparing the new Firefox pages, the old Firefox pages and Chrome's equivalents; and a live study comparing new and old messages with Firefox users.
insight: The usability study found that the word 'connection' misled people into thinking their internet connection was the problem rather than a bad certificate. Jargon like 'security credentials' and 'encrypted' didn't help people understand.
change: New copy and design: plain language with 'certificate' explained on first use, 'connection' removed from headings, short scannable text, and a design that makes the safe choice the clear default while still letting people proceed.
outcome: In the survey, people shown the redesigned pages were 22–50% less likely to say they would try to ignore the warning, and 29–60% less likely to say they would open the site in another browser (4.7–8.5% for new Firefox pages vs 10–11.3% for Chrome's). The live study found no significant negative effect on usage or retention, which cleared the pages for release to all users.
attribution: Fairly direct. The tested copy changes came from the usability findings and published warning research, and the survey compared the new pages against the old ones.
caveats: The headline numbers are stated intentions in a survey panel, not observed behaviour. Ranges are given without per-message detail or sample sizes. The live study only shows no harm. Written by the Mozilla content strategist who worked on it.

sources.title: Designing Better Security Warnings

title: Mozilla's Indonesia research pivots a shopping wish-list idea into a screenshot app
summary: Mozilla's Taipei team set out to build a shopping tool for Indonesia and favoured a cross-app wish list. Surveys of about 200 online shoppers per round, followed by field tests with eight people, kept showing the same surprise: Indonesians screenshot almost everything. The team dropped the wish-list framing and built Firefox ScreenshotGo, an Android app for capturing, finding and acting on screenshots.
problem: In 2018 Mozilla wanted to grow its impact on online shopping in Southeast Asia, starting in Indonesia, a market the team barely knew, with six weeks to define a product.
research: Existing interviews by a Mozilla researcher and desk research fed a shopping journey map. The team then ran several mobile surveys through a local panel (around 200 online shoppers each), storyboard surveys of three wish-list concepts, and a field trip in Indonesia: four interviews on screenshot behaviour, a day of iteration, then prototype tests with four more people.
insight: Screenshots were the dominant tool for keeping wish lists, promotions, shopping history and more, because apps beat websites on experience and price and patchy, costly data made an offline image more reliable than a link. People then struggled to find the right screenshot among countless images and couldn't act on the information in it.
change: The team shaped the product around screenshots instead of a wish list: Firefox ScreenshotGo, an Android app to capture and organise screenshots and get back to related content online, released in the Indonesian Google Play store.
outcome: The product direction changed and an app shipped in Indonesia. The post reports no adoption or usage numbers.
attribution: Direct for the pivot: the post says the screenshot finding was 'out of our expectation' and that the validated findings shaped ScreenshotGo's blueprint.
caveats: Written by the team's designer. No outcome data, and the post doesn't say how the app performed. Small field sample (eight people). 2018.

sources.title: A bumpy road to Firefox ScreenshotGo in a foreign market

title: Concept tests and a diary study reshape Firefox for iOS's chronological tabs
summary: The Firefox for iOS team wanted to know if ordering tabs by time would help people stay on top of open tasks. A prototype test with 10 people, then a three-day diary study with 10 more using a beta build, showed people already thought about tabs in terms of time. The rounds led to date labels, easier tab deletion, and the finding that the whole tab card (thumbnail, title, URL, date) is what helped people resume tasks.
problem: On phones, tabs are ordered by when they were opened, with new tabs from links inserted next to their parent. With many tabs open, finding the one you need is hard.
research: April 2020: concept evaluation of a prototype with 10 US adults (half Firefox users, half Safari or Chrome users). Then a diary study with 10 new participants in Canada and the US who used a beta build as their main browser for three days, answered daily surveys, and were interviewed afterwards.
insight: Participants naturally described their tabs by time and found the chronological order helpful, especially for recent tabs. They wanted to delete single tabs and batches easily. In real use, the combination of thumbnail, title, URL and date stamp jogged people's memory of unfinished tasks. Missing thumbnails and enlarged system text (truncating titles) broke the design.
change: After the first round the team added dates to 'Today' and 'Yesterday', renamed 'Older' to 'Last Week', and made tab deletion easier to reach. After the diary study it prioritised fixing thumbnail loading, and planned research on Android, tablet and desktop plus accessibility work for large text.
outcome: Design changes and a further research plan. No usage metrics are reported.
attribution: Direct: each design change is described as coming from a specific research round.
caveats: Small samples. The post describes a feature still in beta, with no shipped outcome data. Mozilla's own blog.

sources.title: Ordering Browser Tabs Chronologically to Support Task Continuity

title: Airbnb picks a host-to-host marketplace for co-hosting after testing three rough concepts
summary: Airbnb wanted to help people who had a space but couldn't host it themselves. Designers showed potential hosts three deliberately vague 'sacrificial' concepts: an Airbnb-branded professional service, a directory of hospitality partners, and a marketplace of community hosts. Feedback pointed to the marketplace, which was then piloted by hand in Tokyo before becoming the Co-hosting product. Airbnb says inquiries grew from a trickle to a 'torrent' before any promotion.
problem: Host growth lagged guest growth because hosting is hard work, and many would-be hosts couldn't keep up with cleaning, check-ins and guest messages.
research: Around 2015–16, Airbnb's experience designers tested three sacrificial concepts with potential hosts, then storyboarded and prototyped the journey. They ran a service prototype in Tokyo, where the operations team manually matched real hosts and co-hosts by email, forms and spreadsheets, then expanded the pilot to Toronto, Chicago and Washington, D.C., with frequent qualitative testing alongside funnel metrics.
insight: Hosts wanted the reliability of a professional, trusted brand together with the personal attention, local knowledge and entrepreneurial drive of an individual host, and saw property management companies as too volume-focused. The Tokyo pilot confirmed that nearby co-hosts with local expertise and a personal connection were the most wanted, and helped shape messaging, pricing and packaging.
change: Airbnb built Co-hosting as a marketplace connecting hosts with nearby co-hosts from its own community, with search by location and profiles highlighting each co-host's approach and expertise, instead of a professional service or partner directory.
