outcome: The post says inquiries for hosting services went from a trickle to 'a torrent' before co-hosting was promoted or deeply integrated into the main product. No numbers are given, and the author says it is still early.
attribution: Direct for the choice of model: the post ties it to the concept-test feedback and the Tokyo pilot. The demand claim follows the launch but isn't isolated from other factors.
caveats: Airbnb's own design blog, written by the lead designer. No figures. Published in 2016, when the service was still in pilot cities.

sources.title: Co-hosting: Designing a service to support community collaboration

title: Uber's in-car prototype tests in Mexico fix a payment flow drivers 'completed' without paying
summary: When riders in Mexico pay drivers in cash, drivers owe Uber its service fee, and the old process was an emailed invoice. An Uber design and research team spent two weeks with drivers in Mexico City and Guadalajara and tested an in-app payment prototype in parked cars. Drivers raced through the screens and reached 'pending' without ever paying, then planned to call support. The team redesigned the flow with education, restart and code access before rolling it out to several markets.
problem: Drivers with a high volume of cash trips could go into negative balance. Uber collected the fees by emailing invoice links, which was manual for operations, opaque, and easy for drivers to miss.
research: Around 2019–2020, two designers, a product manager and a UX researcher spent two weeks with drivers in Mexico City and Guadalajara (with research trips to Brazil too). They interviewed drivers and tested a Figma prototype on an Android phone in the driver's own car holder.
insight: Drivers didn't understand how cash service fees worked. In testing, many tapped briskly through the steps without reading, reached the 'pending' screen and assumed they had paid, even though they had never gone to a convenience store. Some said they would phone support straight away to ask why the payment was still processing.
change: The team built an in-app collection flow giving drivers control over when and how much to pay, with step-by-step instructions, information before the flow, contextual help on first use, and the ability to restart, cancel, or see their payment code from the 'pending' screen. Copy was localised with local help rather than translated at the end.
outcome: The redesigned flow went on to be released in several markets, including Mexico, Brazil, India and Japan. No metrics are given.
attribution: Direct for the design changes: the post traces the restart and code-access features to the specific failure seen in prototype tests.
caveats: Uber's design blog, written by the product designer. No numbers on payment completion or support calls. Exact research dates not given.

sources.title: Designing For A Cash Experience

title: Wayfair's supplier research puts 'Build the Best Listing' on its global roadmap
summary: Wayfair's supplier technology team wanted to understand the businesses selling through its marketplace beyond the transaction. A survey-based segmentation of all suppliers, a three-week online ethnography with ten suppliers, and stakeholder narratives showed that improving product listings was a key, badly served job. 'Build the Best Listing' was prioritised in the H2 2022 Global Supplier Technology roadmap ahead of new features.
problem: Wayfair's B2B suppliers vary widely in size, business model and roles, which made their needs and motivations hard to understand, and the experience for them affects the end-customer experience.
research: Over about a year to 2022: an online survey to all suppliers, clustered into three segments by firmographics (three months, one researcher plus an external market research firm); a three-week online ethnographic board (Recollective) with ten suppliers doing tasks about why they use Wayfair's Partner Home; and narratives built with subject-matter experts. A six-week design sprint with 40+ people followed to set a north-star vision.
insight: 'Improving listings' is a key job suppliers want to get done on Wayfair and is highly underserved. Needs also differ by company size, headquarters location and whether a supplier is a distributor or manufacturer.
change: 'Build the Best Listing', focused on the product-addition experience, was prioritised in the H2 2022 Global Supplier Technology roadmap over new features. The segmentation is used to send new suppliers personalised communications.
outcome: A roadmap decision and a supplier experience vision. The author says the segmentation helped improve supplier satisfaction and loyalty, especially among smaller businesses, but gives no figures.
attribution: Direct for the roadmap priority, which the post attributes to the research finding. The satisfaction claim is unsupported by data in the post.
caveats: Written by Wayfair's user research lead for the area. No outcome metrics. The listing work's results aren't reported.

sources.title: Building Empathy with Wayfair Suppliers

title: Instacart's 2020 research found many new users were seniors, leading to a senior support line
summary: When the pandemic hit, Instacart's research team rebuilt its roadmap around four workstreams on customer sentiment, experience, expectations and who the new customers were. It found that many new users were seniors or family members ordering for them, that customers wanted truly contactless handoffs, and that new customers were calling support instead of using the help centre. Instacart launched a Senior Support Service, contactless delivery and a help-centre redesign.
problem: In early 2020 Instacart saw larger orders and a huge spike in first-time users, with limited delivery slots and stock problems. It didn't know who the new customers were or what they expected.
research: In 2020 Instacart's research team (with the Consumer Insights and Marketing Research team) re-prioritised into four remote workstreams: customer sentiment, post-order experience, online shopping expectations, and understanding new customers. The post doesn't detail methods or sample sizes.
insight: Many new users were senior citizens, or relatives ordering for them, who chose Instacart as the safer option. Customers wanted an option for a fully contactless drop-off. New customers called the support line instead of using self-help, and the help centre didn't let them solve problems directly.
change: Instacart launched a Senior Support Service (high-touch support for customers over 60), rolled out contactless delivery across the board, and redesigned the help centre to link people to pages where they can fix issues themselves.
outcome: Features launched. The post reports no metrics for them.
attribution: The research manager says the Senior Support Service was 'one example of a feature launch based on these insights'. Contactless delivery was also an industry-wide pandemic response, so research was one input among many.
caveats: Instacart's own design blog. Methods are described only at a high level. Pandemic conditions pushed every delivery company the same way.

sources.title: Research in Unprecedented Times

title: Google's 46 studies behind Material 3 Expressive: key buttons spotted up to 4x faster
summary: Google's Material Design team spent three years and 46 studies, with more than 18,000 participants, testing a more 'expressive' design system. In a lab eye-tracking study comparing 10 apps in expressive and standard versions, people spotted key UI elements up to four times faster, and older users caught up with younger ones. The research also caught expressive designs that hurt usability, which shaped the system's rules.
problem: A 2022 intern study of sentiment toward Material Design in Google apps raised the question of why the apps all looked so similar and dull. The team wanted to know whether more emotional design could also be usable.
research: From 2022 to 2025: 46 studies with 18,000+ participants worldwide, including surveys and focus groups on emotional response, usability tests on speed and comprehension, component-level studies (progress indicators, button size, a floating toolbar), and a lab study with eye-tracking glasses where people used 10 apps in Material 3 Expressive and standard Material 3 versions in random order.
insight: Well-applied expressive design was preferred across ages, by up to 87% among 18–24-year-olds. In eye tracking, larger, more prominent key actions were found up to four times faster (for example, an email Send button), and age differences in fixation time largely disappeared for users over 45. But expressive designs that broke familiar patterns, such as a scattered album-art playlist or email actions without text labels, scored worse on usability.
change: Google shipped Material 3 Expressive in 2025 with new components and guidelines that emphasise size, colour, shape and containment for key actions, while telling teams to keep standard patterns and labels where removing them hurt usability.
outcome: Lab results: key elements spotted up to 4x faster and tap times on key actions reduced 'by seconds'. Surveys found 32% higher 'subculture', 34% higher 'modernity' and 30% higher 'rebelliousness' ratings. No in-product business metrics are reported.
headline_metric: Up to 4x faster to spot key UI
attribution: Direct: the design system was developed and iterated through these studies, and the eye-tracking study compared versions directly.
caveats: 'Up to' four times is a best case across apps. Lab and survey results, not live product metrics. The authors note unfamiliarity affected results, and a strong minority preferred calmer designs. Google writing about its own design system.

sources.title: The research behind Google's bold new direction for design

title: Riding with drivers in Delhi and Jakarta led Google Maps to build a two-wheeler mode
summary: Google Maps researchers went to India and Indonesia to understand fast-growing cities and found Maps was built for cars while millions got around on motorbikes and scooters. They rode with drivers, ran a workshop with Go-Jek riders, and kept testing routes with local partners. The result was two-wheeler mode, the first new transport mode in Google Maps in years, with bike-friendly shortcuts, landmarks and arrival times.
problem: In Delhi and Jakarta, two-wheelers are the most practical way through heavy traffic, but Google Maps offered no routes or arrival times for them and often suggested roads two-wheelers couldn't use.
research: Before mid-2018, a cross-disciplinary team (research, engineering, design, product, marketing) did immersion research in Jaipur, Delhi, Bangalore and Jakarta: interviews in transport hubs and homes, riding along with drivers, and a workshop with Go-Jek drivers (day timelines, pros and cons, co-sketching). Local partners then tested routing, arrival times, landmarks and navigation during development.
insight: Riders navigated in many ways (memorising routes, voice guidance, listening to passengers, phones stuck to the speedometer). Shortcuts and landmarks made navigation faster and safer. Car routes and arrival times were wrong for bikes, and drivers relied on each other as a community when lost.
change: Google launched two-wheeler mode on Android in India and Indonesia (named 'two-wheeler' in India and 'motor' in Indonesia to match local usage), with two-wheeler routes and shortcuts, arrival times, more landmarks and improved voice navigation in more languages. Design principles from the fieldwork also guided other Maps improvements in both countries.
outcome: A new transport mode shipped. The post gives no usage or accuracy figures.
attribution: Strong: the authors credit the field research with defining the product, and local testers caught unsuitable roads and missing landmarks.
caveats: Written by the Google researcher and designer involved. No metrics. The market need may have been visible from data too; the post doesn't compare.

sources.title: Designing Google Maps for Motorbikes

title: FT Edit's in-app survey drives a print cross-promotion and shapes its move into the main FT app
summary: The Financial Times ran a continuous in-app survey in FT Edit, its cheaper eight-articles-a-day app. Moving the survey into a carousel card raised responses 130%. Answers showed one in five readers had recently read the print FT Weekend and that readers feared paywalls and losing the focused format if FT Edit moved into the main FT app. That led to a print campaign in FT Weekend and a dedicated, carousel-based FT Edit space in the main app.
problem: FT Edit launched in 2022 with a feedback survey tucked in Settings, and responses had slowed. The team needed steady insight on who its readers were, and later on the risks of folding FT Edit into the main FT app on a tight timeline.
research: From 2022 an ongoing in-app survey, later moved to a repurposed carousel card that appeared sparingly and could be dismissed. Questions covered who FT Edit readers are, why they read it, what they want more or less of, and which other FT products they use, plus a later question on concerns about merging into the main app.
insight: One in five FT Edit readers had read the print FT Weekend in the past month, which usage data couldn't show, and they were less likely to work in financial services than full FT subscribers. Many wanted more choice. Ahead of the merge, respondents worried about regularly hitting paywalled stories and losing the focused reading experience.
change: The FT ran an experimental print marketing campaign for FT Edit inside FT Weekend, trialled recommendation-engine articles alongside the editorial picks, and designed a dedicated FT Edit space in the main FT app that opens automatically for FT Edit subscribers, shields them from paywalled stories, and keeps FT Edit's one-article-at-a-time horizontal carousel.
outcome: Survey response rate rose 130% after the move to the carousel card. The FT describes the FT Weekend print campaign as 'successful' but gives no figures. The merge design was 'directly influenced' by survey feedback. Personalisation trials were small due to time and technical limits.
attribution: Direct for the decisions, which the author ties to specific survey findings. The 130% figure measures the research method (survey placement), not a product outcome.
caveats: Written by the FT researcher who ran the survey. No metrics for the print campaign or the merged experience. Survey respondents are self-selected.

sources.title: Guiding Strategy: How an in-app survey supported product iteration

title: Tokopedia's interviews and post-launch tests shape its phone trade-in and raise purchase completion
summary: Tokopedia researched why people kept old phones unused or struggled to resell them, using interviews, a survey and competitor research, and built Tukar Tambah, a trade-in where the app values your old phone and a courier swaps it for the new one. After a limited launch, interviews and usability tests found the purchase journey too long and price estimates too inaccurate. Tokopedia says fixes significantly raised purchase completion over the next two quarters, but gives no numbers.
problem: Many Indonesians buy a new phone often, and old phones pile up unused because reselling them is a hassle.
research: Early stage: in-depth interviews on triggers and barriers when buying a new phone and selling an old one, a survey to size the problems, and desk research benchmarking competitors. Before launch: usability testing of the trade-in flow. After a limited launch: evaluation research with in-depth interviews and usability testing on the live product.
insight: The top validated problem was helping people sell their old phone quickly so they could put the money toward a new one. After launch, users wanted a shorter purchase journey and more accurate price indications.
change: Tokopedia built Tukar Tambah: choose a new phone, let the app scan the old phone and estimate its value in rupiah, pay the difference, and a courier delivers the new phone and collects the old one. After the evaluation research the team shortened the purchase journey and worked on pricing accuracy.
outcome: The author says purchase completion rose 'significantly' in the first two quarters after launch, and the number of trade-ins kept growing as the feature expanded. No figures are given.
attribution: Moderate. The post links the improvements to research feedback, but completion gains in the first months after a launch have many possible causes.
caveats: Written by a Tokopedia researcher as an argument for research. No numbers, no control. Dates of the work aren't given.

sources.title: How User Research plays Important Keys to Unlock Minimum Lovable Product for Customers

title: GitLab click tests: moving the clone button lifted findability from 84% to 98%
summary: After a redesign hid GitLab's clone options in the page header, users asked for the button back near the file tree. A designer ran quick click tests against the live design before deciding. The proposed spot was found by 98% of testers versus 84% for the live one, and a second test showed that removing the button from empty repositories would drop success to 50%, so the team kept one there.
problem: GitLab's 2019 project overview redesign put a single clone button in the page header, which removed it from the repository page. Users suggested moving it down to the file tree controls, but the team had already had complaints about the earlier change and worried that moving it lower would make it harder to find.
research: Two unmoderated click tests (UsabilityHub), each run as two variants: the proposed design and the live design as a control. Around 40 answers per variant. The UX research team helped word the task so it did not use the word 'clone'. A second pair of tests checked the empty-repository page with and without a clone button.
insight: Moving the button down to the file tree did not hurt findability, it improved it: people expected it there, as on other Git platforms. On empty repositories, though, removing the button badly hurt findability.
change: The clone button moved to the file tree controls and returned to the repository page. A clone button was added above the instructions on the empty-repository page rather than dropped.
outcome: Proposed file-tree position: 98% correct, 15 seconds on average. Live header position: 84% correct, 21 seconds. Empty repository without a button: 50% correct, 37 seconds, versus 77% and 16 seconds with the button. At publication the change was being built by a community contributor.
attribution: Direct for the decision: the post says the tests drove both choices. The numbers are test results, not live product metrics after launch.
caveats: Small unmoderated samples (about 40 per variant) and a single click task, with no statistical testing reported. No post-launch data. Written by the designer who ran the tests on GitLab's own blog.

sources.title: Quantifying UX: Positioning the clone button

title: GitLab dropped its first navigation fixes after research, then rebuilt around diary studies
summary: GitLab users kept calling its navigation confusing. The team's first proposed fixes did poorly in research, so it went back to study how people actually move around GitLab, using diary studies, card sorts and repeated concept tests. The 2023 navigation added pinning and task-based sidebar groups, and a month-long study found users preferred it.
problem: Users said GitLab's navigation was complex and confusing. Early solutions the team researched would not have helped users enough to be worth shipping, and the team did not understand why the navigation was failing.
research: Review of past research and System Usability Scale feedback; diary studies with cohorts of key personas; several rounds of solution validation tests on design concepts; facilitated card sorts on sidebar groupings; then a month-long longitudinal study with interviews and surveys at the start, middle and end, while the new navigation was an opt-in toggle. Roughly 2022–2023.
insight: Many users barely navigate inside GitLab because they arrive via links from Slack, email and other tools. Their work is narrowly scoped, so they wanted quick access to a few core features, and they used workarounds such as bookmarks and open tabs. Card sorts showed people wanted analytics items grouped together.
change: GitLab stopped pursuing its earlier proposed fixes and built a new navigation around three themes from the feedback (less overwhelm, better orientation, picking up where you left off). It added pinning, task-based sidebar categories and a new Analyze section, and shipped with an on/off toggle.
outcome: Participants in the longitudinal study found the new navigation an improvement and preferred its features, especially pinning and the task-based sidebar. They also raised problems, such as not being able to pin whole projects and unpinning items by accident. No usage or satisfaction numbers are given.
attribution: Strong for the decisions: the posts trace the abandoned fixes, the pinning feature and the sidebar groupings to specific studies. The outcome is qualitative.
caveats: Company blog posts with no numbers on adoption or satisfaction; a quarterly navigation survey was set up but results are not reported. Community reaction to redesigns is mixed and not covered here.

sources.title: How we overhauled GitLab navigation
Inside the vision for GitLab's new platform navigation

title: Duolingo interviews about learners' mistakes led to the Practice Hub
summary: Duolingo's researchers interviewed learners about how they think about the mistakes they make. Learners wanted to see past mistakes and drill their weak areas. Duolingo says this research was the inspiration for the Practice Hub, a paid feature for reviewing mistakes and practising skills.
problem: Duolingo wanted to understand what learners need beyond new lessons, and specifically how they relate to the errors they make.
research: A series of one-on-one UX interviews with learners about their mistakes. Participant numbers and dates are not given.
insight: Learners wanted to know which mistakes they had made in past lessons and to practise their 'weak areas'. One learner described repeatedly forgetting verb forms for a tense.
change: Duolingo built the Practice Hub, a subscription feature that gathers past mistakes for targeted practice and adds speaking and listening practice.
outcome: The feature shipped as part of Duolingo's paid tier. No usage, retention or revenue figures are given.
attribution: The company names the research as 'the inspiration' for the feature. How much the interviews shaped the final design is not described.
caveats: A short example inside a general post written for learners, not a case study. No metrics. The feature also sits behind a paywall, so the company had a commercial reason to build it.

sources.title: How our learners (that's you!) help improve Duolingo

title: Slack built Activity 2.0 around four triage habits found in research
summary: Slack's Activity tab was popular but only held some notifications and could only mark them read. Research into how people triage found four distinct habits that the same person switches between. Slack rebuilt Activity to support all of them and reports an 80% engagement rate for the new version.
problem: Activity, launched in Slack's 2023 redesign, became the second most-used surface, but people still jumped between surfaces to catch up. It lacked some notification types and only let people mark items as read.
research: User research on how people manage and triage notifications, combined with usage data, pilots with different kinds of companies and rapid internal testing of functional prototypes. Participant numbers are not given.
insight: There is no single triage style. People move between keeping a curated inbox, moving items to other task tools, skimming, and clearing unreads, depending on context. Notification volume also changes what people need: large-team users need different tools from small-team users.
change: Activity 2.0 brings DMs, mentions, threads, reminders, reactions and key channel notifications into one feed, with a simple default and optional filters, saved views, keyboard navigation and bulk actions for heavy users.
outcome: Slack reports an 80% engagement rate for the new experience, and that 60% of engaged Activity users are starting to triage and recall DMs from Activity. It also says some users struggled to leave familiar workflows.
attribution: Partial. The triage insight clearly shaped the design, but the engagement numbers are not compared with Activity 1.0 and no method is given.
caveats: 'Engagement rate' is not defined and there is no baseline. Company design blog post, written partly to showcase the team's process.

sources.title: No small task: Evolving the way millions catch up in Slack

title: Figma reversed UI3's floating panels after beta feedback showed they slowed people down
summary: Figma's UI3 redesign put the main side panels in floating windows over the canvas. During the open beta, feedback, adoption and performance data showed the panels cramped the canvas and slowed down people who work in Figma all day. Figma re-docked the panels for the general release and reverted a few other beta changes.
problem: Figma spent over two years on UI3 and chose floating navigation and properties panels for a simpler look, knowing it might be too big a change for heavy users.
research: An open beta with an opt-out, monitored through feature adoption, performance metrics and user feedback. The post does not describe formal studies or sample sizes.
insight: The floating panels hindered people who spend many hours a day in Figma: they cramped the canvas, especially on small screens, designs peeked out distractingly behind them, rulers sat further from the work, and they slowed people down. A dropdown for 'clip content' also added a click that slowed workflows.
change: For the October 2024 full rollout, the navigation and properties panels became fixed (but resizable). Clip content went back to a checkbox, and constraints were expanded by default. Floating panels stayed only in Minimize UI, Figma Slides grid view and FigJam.
outcome: A core design decision was reversed before general release. No metrics are shared.
attribution: Clear that beta feedback and data drove the reversal ('the nail in the coffin was learning that they slowed people down'). The evidence came from a beta rather than planned research.
caveats: Evidence is beta feedback and product analytics rather than structured research, and no numbers are given. Company blog post; heavy public criticism of the floating panels on Figma's forum was likely also a factor.

sources.title: Figma on Figma: Our approach to designing UI3

title: Monzo added home screen customisation after early concepts confused customers
summary: Monzo's app had outgrown its design, so it spent over a year redesigning the home screen, hearing from more than 1,000 customers along the way. Early concepts were called overwhelming and confusing; customers wanted control over what they see, which became the customisation feature. Research also led Monzo to let people snooze the switch to the new design.
problem: After adding many products (Plus, Premium, Flex, savings pots, external accounts), customers could not easily discover features or see their full financial picture on Monzo's home screen.
research: Customer research throughout a project of more than a year, with input from over 1,000 customers, alongside Monzo Community feedback and 4 major and 2 minor experiments over 7 months. Specific methods are not detailed.
insight: Early concepts felt overwhelming and confusing. Customers wanted to choose what appears on their home screen. Interrupting people with the new design while they were trying to do a task went badly.
change: Monzo built customisation into the new home screen, kept core jobs (balances, card details, transaction search) prominent, and let customers snooze the upgrade and be prompted later.
outcome: The new home screen rolled out to more than 8 million customers. No outcome metrics are shared.
attribution: The user researcher names customisation as a direct result of research. No outcome data is linked to it.
caveats: Short company post with quotes from team members; methods, sample breakdowns and experiment results are not given.

sources.title: How we built the new Home screen, by the people who got us here

title: Microsoft's EEG study of back-to-back meetings led to Outlook settings that build in breaks
summary: Microsoft's Human Factors Lab had 14 people do video meetings while wearing EEG caps, once back-to-back and once with 10-minute breaks. Stress-linked brain activity built up without breaks and stayed flat with them. Microsoft says the findings helped inform Outlook settings that automatically shorten meetings to leave breaks, including organisation-wide defaults.
problem: During the pandemic, back-to-back video meetings became normal and people reported meeting fatigue. Microsoft wanted to know whether short breaks made a measurable difference.
research: A within-subjects lab study: 14 volunteers wore EEG caps through two sessions of four 30-minute video meetings on consecutive Mondays, one with no breaks and one with 10-minute meditation breaks (Headspace), with order swapped between groups.
insight: Without breaks, beta-wave activity (associated with stress) kept building and spiked at transitions between meetings, and frontal alpha asymmetry suggested people were less engaged. With breaks, stress stayed level and engagement was higher.
change: Microsoft promoted Outlook settings that shave 5, 10 or 15 minutes off meetings, and added organisation-wide defaults so a company can build in breaks for everyone.
outcome: The settings shipped for individuals and organisations in 2021. No data on adoption or effect on wellbeing is given.
attribution: Microsoft says the findings 'helped inform' the settings. Adjustable meeting lengths may have been in the works anyway; the study mainly justified and publicised them.
caveats: Very small sample (14), lab setting, and EEG proxies for stress and engagement. Published as a marketing-led Work Trend Index piece. No measure of whether the product change reduced fatigue.

sources.title: Research Proves Your Brain Needs Breaks

title: HubSpot card sorts showed no one grouped its apps by its own marketing methodology
summary: HubSpot's product navigation was organised around its Inbound Marketing methodology, and support staff confirmed customers got lost. In about 6.5 hours of card sorting and quick usability tests, not one participant, including long-time customers, grouped the apps by the methodology. HubSpot switched to an object-based navigation.
problem: HubSpot's apps had long been organised by the stages of its Inbound Marketing methodology. As the product grew this became hard to extend, and it had been debated internally for years.
research: Conversations with Support and Services staff about customers getting lost; open card sorts with HubSpot's own marketing team (about four sessions); remote card sorts of about 20 cards with four customers; then usability tests of three low-fidelity layouts plus the existing navigation with three customers and three non-customers. About 6.5 hours of testing in total, in 2012.
insight: Support confirmed customers got lost and filed cases about finding apps. In testing, an object-based layout was most intuitive, and none of the participants, even customers who had embraced inbound marketing, organised the apps by the methodology.
change: HubSpot replaced the methodology-based menu with an object-based navigation, released first to beta customers and then to all users.
outcome: The post was written at beta launch. It expected fewer support cases about finding apps but reports no results.
attribution: Strong for the decision: the post credits the tests with settling a long internal debate. No outcome data.
caveats: Very small samples (four customers in the card sort, six people in the usability test). Old (2012). No follow-up numbers were published in this post. Company blog.

sources.title: The New HubSpot Nav Bar Design: A Web App Usability Study

title: HubSpot's usability baseline found users missed filters and saved views, so it redesigned its busiest pages
summary: HubSpot's CRM index pages are used by more than 96% of daily users, but a 2019 usability baseline study found many people never noticed filtering, saved views or column editing. Combined with usage data and old bug tickets, this led to a redesign with saved-view tabs, quick filters and visible column editing.
problem: The Contacts, Companies, Deals and Tickets index pages are HubSpot's most-used pages, but after a service outage the team took a hard look and found customers did not like using them.
research: Usability baseline studies of the Sales and Service Hubs in early 2019; a review of past Jira tickets closed as 'works as designed'; usage analytics; interaction-flow mapping; customer conversations, concept testing and several rounds of usability testing over some months.
insight: Many users never noticed that filtering was possible, and saving views, sorting and adding columns were rarely found. Related controls, like search and filters, sat far apart. Usage data showed users who save and revisit a view have 16% higher week-12 retention, yet only 5% of new users touched saved views in their first month and only 15% of daily users saved one.
change: The redesigned table view added tabs for saved views, quick filters based on the most-used properties, and column editing on the main screen. The board view got its own layout with pipeline and saved-view toggles up front.
outcome: Released as an opt-in experience in 2020. No post-launch results are reported.
attribution: The post ties each design change to a usability or analytics finding. There is no outcome data.
caveats: Company product blog with an opt-in launch and no reported results. The 16% retention link for saved views is correlational. Usability study sample sizes are not given.

sources.title: Overhauling the Index Page

title: Interviews with 50+ artists led Adobe to build Fresco instead of extending its two drawing apps
summary: Adobe had two free drawing apps and had to choose between improving them or building something new. Months of interviews with more than 50 artists, followed by alpha testing with 10 hand-picked illustrators and regular usability sessions, led to Adobe Fresco, which combines pixel and vector drawing. Testing also changed specific features, such as where tool options sit and a new Touch Shortcut.
problem: Adobe Photoshop Sketch and Illustrator Draw were used for professional work, but customers wanted Photoshop and Illustrator features in them. Adobe had to decide whether to keep iterating on both or build a new app.
research: Several months of interviews with more than 50 artists and illustrators across 11 illustration categories and many countries, chosen to cover the popular apps in each. Then a three-month alpha with 10 illustrators ('Gemini 10') doing workflow tasks on early builds; feature usability sessions with at least three professionals and three emerging artists, including non-Adobe users; group sessions three to four times a year; student sessions; and a prerelease community of over 600 artists. Roughly 2017–2020.
insight: Customisation was a big reason people love Adobe's desktop tools, and keyboard shortcuts are central to fast work, but few iPad artists use keyboards. Testers said Fresco felt a little slow. Very few noticed tool options placed directly below the tool, while floating options were easy to find but took canvas space.
change: Adobe built Fresco as a new app combining pixels and vectors, with a customisable app frame. It added a Touch Shortcut that temporarily changes the current tool's action, and docked tool options at the bottom of the toolbar with the option to drag them anywhere. Some early experiences were reworked after poor test results.
outcome: Fresco launched in 2019 and kept evolving with monthly releases. No usage or business metrics are given.
attribution: The article says the decision to create Fresco 'grew from extensive user research' and links specific features to test findings. No outcome data.
caveats: Promotional company article timed with product updates. Adobe also had strategic reasons (competing on iPad) that the article does not weigh. No metrics.

sources.title: The creation and evolution of Adobe Fresco

title: Designing Visual Studio IntelliCode with developers who struggle to focus tripled regular use
summary: Microsoft's developer tools team recruited developers by cognitive need, including people with and without ADHD who find it hard to focus, rather than by language or background. They found IntelliCode's suggestions appeared too fast and its hint bar was hard to find. Co-designed changes gave users more control over when suggestions appear, and Microsoft reports a 3.5x increase in regular users of one feature.
problem: The team needed to balance making AI code suggestions discoverable against interrupting developers, and to find the most helpful way to present suggestions.
research: Inclusive design research and co-design sessions with existing users, recruited around the cognitive demand of focus (developers with and without ADHD). Sample size and dates are not given.
insight: The tool's interruptions made concentration hard: code suggestions appeared automatically too quickly, and the hint bar took a lot of work to find.
change: The team co-designed changes that give developers more control over when intelligent suggestions surface, for both inline code insertion suggestions and single-line code change suggestions.
outcome: Microsoft reports a 3.5x increase in regular users of inline code insertion suggestions. Testing of the enhanced single-line code change suggestions showed a 176% increase in suggestions accepted and a 29% increase in regular users.
attribution: The case study links the changes to the research, but it does not say how the numbers were measured, over what period, or whether other changes shipped at the same time.
caveats: Short promotional case study in Microsoft's inclusive design toolkit, with no method, baseline or dates for the numbers. 'Testing' may mean an A/B test, but this is not stated.

sources.title: Microsoft Inclusive Design for Cognition: Case Studies (PDF)

title: Duolingo's interviews in India led to everyday Hindi wording and dropping its subscription, lifting active users 6%
summary: As newly online learners poured into Duolingo in India in 2020, research showed its Hindi interface used formal words even native speakers found hard, and that people mistook the Duolingo Plus promotion for a paywall and preferred one-off payments. A/B tests of the fixes lifted onboarding completion by 1%, and removing Duolingo Plus in India raised daily active users by 6%.
problem: New learners in India grew 400% year on year, many of them online for the first time. Duolingo's app had been built for markets where people had different language habits and were used to app subscriptions.
research: User research with learners in India, including interviews, alongside usage data, followed by A/B tests of each change. The post does not say how the tap-through behaviour was spotted, and gives no participant numbers or dates.
insight: Duolingo's Hindi was technically correct but uncommon in everyday speech: interviewees called the in-app currency 'coin' or 'diamond', not the Hindi word used, and English words like 'level' and 'language' were more natural. New learners tended to tap the most prominent button, so they read the Duolingo Plus promotion as a paywall and quit, and several said they would prefer a one-time fee to a subscription.
change: Onboarding swapped some Hindi words for the common English ones, written in English. Duolingo first removed the early Plus promotion for new learners, then removed Duolingo Plus entirely in India and a few other Asian countries, choosing growth before monetisation.
outcome: The wording change gave a 1% increase in onboarding completion. Removing the early Plus promotion gave a 1% increase in daily active users; removing Plus altogether gave a 6% increase. (A separate data-led change, putting the English course at the top of the list, added 2% to daily active users.)
attribution: Good: each change was A/B tested, and the post ties the wording and paywall changes to what interviews and observation showed. The decision to drop Plus also reflected a business choice to grow first.
caveats: Short company post with no sample sizes, test durations or significance figures. The 6% gain came from removing a revenue product, so it says nothing about revenue. India-specific, during the 2020 lockdown surge.

sources.title: Language learning for the next billion: Duolingo in India

title: Wikipedia's Reply tool: newer editors far more likely to publish a talk-page comment
summary: Replying on Wikipedia talk pages meant editing raw wikitext, indenting and signing by hand. After a community consultation and usability tests showed newcomers couldn't do it, the Editing team built a one-click Reply tool. A month-long A/B test on 22 Wikipedias found newer editors with the tool published comments far more often and had fewer reverted.
problem: To reply on a talk page, contributors had to edit the whole page's source, find the right spot, indent with colons and sign with tildes. Newer editors often did not know how to reply at all; experienced ones struggled to find the comment they wanted in long threads.
research: The team drew on the 2019 Talk Page Consultation with the editing community, earlier user testing from 2014, and its own usability tests: 5 people on the existing workflow, 5 on a version 1.0 prototype, and later about 10 junior and 13 senior contributors on version 2.0.
insight: In testing the existing workflow, 0 of 5 participants indented and signed their comment correctly. With the prototype, all 5 published a correctly formatted reply in about half the time. The barrier for newcomers was mechanical, not motivation.
change: The team built a Reply link next to each comment that opens a small box and handles indentation and signatures automatically, released it as a beta feature in 2020, then as an opt-out default on several wikis.
outcome: In an A/B test from 11 February to 10 March 2021 on 22 Wikipedias, where half of editors got the tool automatically, 72.9% of Junior Contributors with the tool published at least one comment versus 27.6% without (the team calls it a 160% increase). Junior Contributors were 7.2 times more likely to publish a comment they started, and reverts of their comments fell 79.5%. The team then offered the tool as an opt-out default across Wikimedia projects.
attribution: Strong. The tool was designed to fix problems found in consultation and usability tests, and the outcome comes from a randomized test of that tool.
caveats: The write-up is inconsistent about whether the comparison is people who 'opened' the tool or who 'had access' to it; the figures are the same either way, but the exact denominator is unclear. Results are on talk-page participation, not longer-term editor retention. Some large wikis (including English Wikipedia) were not part of the default rollout at first.

sources.title: Talk pages project/Replying

title: Wikipedia's newcomer homepage: early test showed gains, a 27-wiki trial found small ones
summary: Interviews with new and experienced editors in Korea and the Czech Republic led Wikimedia to form a Growth team and build a 'newcomer homepage' with suggested edits and help. A four-wiki randomized test in 2019–20 reported an 11.6% lift in newcomers making a first edit, but a later 27-wiki controlled experiment found only a small activation effect and no retention gain.
problem: Midsize Wikipedias were not attracting and keeping new editors. Most people who created an account never made an edit, and few came back.
research: From May to July 2017 Wikimedia ran design research with the firm Reboot: 64 in-person interviews (30 on Korean Wikipedia, 34 on Czech Wikipedia) with new editors and the experienced editors who support them.
insight: Newcomers' main obstacles were conceptual rather than technical: they didn't understand policies or 'the Wikipedia way', couldn't find help or editing processes, and often sought help outside Wikipedia. The research recommended in-context help, mentorship and task suggestions based on interests.
change: The research led to the creation of the Growth team in 2018, which built the newcomer homepage, a help panel, mentorship and 'newcomer tasks' that suggest easy edits on topics the person picks.
outcome: A randomized experiment on Arabic, Vietnamese, Czech and Korean Wikipedia (97,755 new accounts, Nov 2019–May 2020) estimated activation (first article edit within 24 hours) rose from 21.6% to 24.1%, an 11.6% increase, with constructive activation up 26.7%; retention changes were not detected directly. A later peer-reviewed randomized experiment across 27 non-English Wikipedias found only a small but significant increase in activation (about 1% higher odds of editing within 24 hours) and no difference in retention, productivity or reverts.
attribution: Moderate. The feature set traces back to the 2017 interview research, and both evaluations were randomized, but neither isolates which research finding drove which feature.
caveats: The two controlled experiments disagree: the larger, later study found much weaker effects than the early pilot. Retention gains in the pilot were inferred, not measured. The homepage seemed to distract newcomers who were already mid-edit. Included as an honest example that a research-led feature can test modestly.

title: New York's redesigned court summons and text reminders cut missed court dates 13–26%
company: New York City Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice, NYPD and Office of Court Administration (with ideas42 and University of Chicago Crime Lab)
summary: About 41% of people given a ticket for a low-level offence in New York missed their court date, triggering an arrest warrant. Researchers interviewed past recipients and redesigned the summons form and added text reminders. Evaluations found the form cut missed appearances by about 13% and the best set of texts by 26%.
problem: In 2014 almost 41% of people who received a summons for a low-level offence in New York City did not appear in court, about 130,000 missed court dates a year, each leading to an arrest warrant. The old form made it hard to pick out the date, time, place and consequences.
research: Over a three-year collaboration, ideas42 and the University of Chicago Crime Lab worked with city agencies and community groups to interview summons recipients, including people who had previously missed court dates, many with inflexible jobs or experience of homelessness. This fed a behavioural diagnosis of why people didn't show up.
insight: Many people did not miss court on purpose: they didn't realise they had to go, forgot, or didn't plan for it. Interviewees also believed most people skip court, when most attend, and that misperception made skipping feel normal.
change: Police switched to a redesigned summons with a clear title saying what to do, the court date, time and location at the top, and the consequence of not appearing. People could give a phone number to receive text reminders 7 days, 3 days and 1 day before court, with wording tested for plan-making and consequences.
outcome: J-PAL's summary reports the new form cut failure to appear by 6.4 percentage points from a 41% baseline (about 13%), roughly 17,000 fewer arrest warrants a year. In a randomized evaluation of about 20,000 recipients, any pre-court text cut failure to appear by 8 points from a 38% control mean (21%), and the best text set by 10 points (26%). The city adopted the new form for all summonses and sends the best-performing texts to everyone who gives a number.
attribution: Strong for the texts (randomized); moderate for the form (quasi-experimental comparison). Interview research shaped the diagnosis and content, though the design also drew heavily on behavioural science theory.
caveats: The form evaluation was not randomized. Only a minority of recipients gave a phone number, so the text results apply to that group. Much of the design rationale is behavioural economics rather than direct usability testing with recipients. Partners ideas42 and the Crime Lab co-authored the evaluation (published in Science, 2020).

title: GOV.UK benchmarking found people stalling at 'Start now'; button-label tests lifted clicks up to 30%
summary: GOV.UK's benchmarking research found users reached the right page but didn't click the green 'Start now' button, looping back instead. The team A/B tested goal-matched labels. Some won clearly (the DVLA contact page's 'Find contact details' raised mobile clicks 30%), but on one page the alternatives lost by up to 18.8%.
problem: Users often landed on the right GOV.UK page but hesitated at the 'Start now' button, ran in-page searches or revisited the page several times. On the overseas passports page, about 30% of users visited multiple times, roughly 52,000 people a month.
research: GOV.UK's fourth benchmarking wave (reported February 2016) had a representative panel attempt common tasks chosen from analytics, then took the worst-performing tasks into lab research days. Analytics on repeat visits backed this up.
insight: The phrase 'Start now' didn't match what people were trying to do. It suggested something more formal or serious, such as starting an application, when they just wanted information or a phone number.
change: The team ran A/B/C tests of alternative button labels on the overseas passports, child maintenance calculator and getting married abroad pages, then on the Contact DVLA page changed 'Start now' to 'Find contact details'. They also removed a distracting link on the child maintenance page that benchmarking showed led to lower completion.
outcome: On overseas passports, 'Next' raised click rate 5.1%; on child maintenance, 'Estimate your child maintenance' raised it 3.5%. On getting married abroad, the alternatives lost: -13.6% and -18.8%. On Contact DVLA, 'Find contact details' increased button clicks 30% on mobile and 14% on desktop, estimated at about 780,000 more successful sessions a year. Removing the child maintenance link raised calculator button clicks 6%.
attribution: Direct. The benchmarking lab research identified the hesitation and the hypothesis; the changes were then A/B tested.
caveats: Results are click rates, not full task completion (the team reports button wording did not change continuation after the click). Effects varied by page and one test lost badly, so there is no universal label. Percentages are relative changes in click rate. Annual impact figures are the team's own extrapolations.

sources.title: Benchmarking GOV.UK and what we are doing with what we found out
Absolutely fabulous testing
Using A/B testing to measurably improve common user journeys

title: GOV.UK's new sign-in choice page nearly doubled clicks on the less-visible option
company: Government Digital Service (GOV.UK) with HM Revenue and Customs
summary: Some government services could be accessed through several sign-in routes, but the start page's single green button favoured one. Research showed people forget how they signed in before and recognise identity-provider brands better than 'GOV.UK Verify'. A one-week A/B test of a new sign-in choice page nearly doubled clicks on Verify without hurting Government Gateway completion.
problem: Services like filing a Self Assessment tax return could be reached through Government Gateway or GOV.UK Verify, but the start page's green button could only point to one, burying the other. The start page had also grown beyond what it was designed for.
research: GOV.UK content designers drew on earlier user research into how people sign in to infrequently used services; the post summarises the findings but does not describe the study design. The new page was then A/B tested.
insight: People who used a service before often didn't remember which sign-in route they had used, especially for once-a-year tasks. People who had verified their identity tended to remember the certified company they spent time with rather than the name 'GOV.UK Verify'.
change: GOV.UK added a 'service sign-in page' between the start page and the service, listing each option with short memory-jogging prompt text and a route for new users.
outcome: In a one-week A/B test in November 2017 on HMRC's Self Assessment service (70% old start page, 30% new design), the Verify link, previously clicked by 4.3% of users, 'nearly doubled' its click rate. Government Gateway completion was unaffected, and on-page searches for 'sign in' and 'log in' fell. The page went live and was rolled out to two more HMRC services.
attribution: Direct but light on detail. The design responds to stated research findings and was A/B tested.
caveats: The post gives no exact post-change figure, sample size or significance. The research behind the insights is described only briefly. Measures choice of sign-in route, not whether more people completed the service. GOV.UK Verify was later wound down.

sources.title: Making it easier for users to sign in to services

title: Task-based testing with 100+ separating parents reshaped GOV.UK family law guidance
summary: A Ministry of Justice content team tested GOV.UK's guidance for separating parents with more than 100 users. Opinion-based sessions said the content was 'fine'; task-based tests showed people couldn't tell whether mediation applied to them. After rewriting the mediation chapter and headings, engagement time rose 74% and the usefulness rating rose from 67% to 80%.
problem: GOV.UK's private family law guidance, used by people divorcing or separating who need to sort out child arrangements, left readers confused, especially about mediation, so they kept searching elsewhere.
research: From September 2024 a content designer, a user researcher and a content lead tested the guidance with more than 100 users, mainly separating parents. Early sessions asked for opinions; the team switched to task-based testing, asking people to find or do something specific.
insight: Asking for opinions hid the problems: people called the content 'good, or fine'. Giving them tasks revealed missing information and that many were unsure whether mediation suited their circumstances. Specific, descriptive headings helped people find things faster.
change: The team published eight rounds of changes: restructured the mediation guidance and explained the process plainly, rewrote headings to be more specific, and revamped the 'apply for a court order' chapter.
outcome: For the mediation chapter, average engagement time per session rose 74%, the page usefulness rating rose from 67% to 80%, and clicks through to find a mediator rose 14%. The team also reports more page views and fewer on-page searches, without figures.
attribution: Direct. The changes respond to task-based testing findings and the metrics are for the rewritten chapter.
caveats: Before/after analytics with no control group and no stated time periods. Longer engagement time is ambiguous as a success measure. 'Usefulness' is a self-selected page feedback rating. Changes shipped in eight tranches, so effects of individual changes can't be separated.

sources.title: How user research transformed GOV.UK guidance for separating families

title: MNbenefits research with Spanish speakers lifted their application completion from 51% to 64%
company: Code for America with Minnesota Department of Human Services
summary: Code for America and Minnesota built MNbenefits, a single online application for nine safety-net programs that cut average application time from nearly an hour to about 15 minutes. When a funnel analysis showed Spanish speakers dropping out at the citizenship question, a translation audit and research sessions with Spanish speakers led to a new follow-up question, and their completion rate rose from 51% to 64%.
problem: Applying for multiple benefits in Minnesota took about an hour. After launch, Spanish-speaking applicants completed the application far less often than English speakers, and many dropped out when asked about U.S. citizenship, even though citizenship is not required for some programs.
research: Discovery (2018–2019) included shadowing and interviewing state and county staff and research with clients. After launch, the team combined funnel analysis with a translation audit and in-person research sessions with Spanish-speaking clients, plus SMS surveys and live-chat feedback.
insight: Spanish speakers were abandoning at the citizenship question, likely fearing it made them ineligible; the translation also had words and phrases that didn't land, which the team worked through page by page with clients.
change: The team added a follow-up question after the citizenship question and reworked the Spanish translation on every page based on the sessions. Separately, client feedback led to changes in document upload.
outcome: Code for America reports the follow-up question 'substantially increased' completion for Spanish speakers from 51% to 64%, narrowing the gap with English speakers (69%). Overall, MNbenefits cut average time to apply from nearly an hour to 15 minutes (saving an average of 47 minutes) and helped more than 240,000 people access over $100 million in benefits in two years.
attribution: Fairly direct for the Spanish-speaker result: the funnel drop-off was diagnosed through research with Spanish speakers and the specific change followed. The headline time saving reflects the whole product, not one finding.
caveats: Before/after comparison with no control group or stated time windows. Self-reported by Code for America, which co-built the service. The overall time saving compares the new application to the legacy one, whose baseline varies across sources (60 to 110 minutes).

sources.title: MNbenefits Report 2022
sources.publisher: Code for America (via Digital Government Hub)

title: GOV.UK cut business start-up guidance from 50+ pages to 16; clicks to registration services rose 25%
company: Government Digital Service (GOV.UK) with Companies House, BEIS and HMRC
summary: GOV.UK's guidance for people starting a business was spread across more than 50 pages owned by different departments. Research showed people only cared about getting compliance tasks done, not who owned them. The team rewrote it as 16 pages; clicks through to business registration services rose 25%.
problem: Guidance for setting up a business was split by department and spread over more than 50 pages, much of it not relevant to someone starting out, making it hard to reach the registration services people needed.
research: The team reviewed existing research and mapped actions, emotions and pain points; analysed search and page-view data to draft user needs; validated them with people setting up businesses; ran cognitive walkthroughs of the existing content; visited business support helpline advisers; and ran repeated research rounds with people starting businesses.
insight: Dealing with government sat at the edge of people's thinking about starting a business and was driven by compliance. They didn't care which department did what and wanted to complete tasks; topics like reporting anti-competitive activity weren't on their minds at all.
change: GDS, Companies House, BEIS and HMRC cut the guidance from more than 50 pages to 16, removed content research showed wasn't working, and rewrote the guidance on choosing a business structure.
outcome: After the change the team saw a 25% increase in clicks to services needed to set up a business (referrals to HMRC registration for sole traders or Companies House for limited companies) and a 5% decrease in average pages per session to reach them. In the final research round, most participants said the business structure guidance made them more confident.
attribution: Direct. The content rewrite was driven by the research and the measures are for the rewritten journey.
caveats: Before/after analytics with no stated time period, sample size or control; seasonality and other changes could contribute. Clicks to a service are not the same as completed registrations.

sources.title: Taking care of business on GOV.UK

title: Google surveyed thousands on browser icons, and Chrome adopted 'Not secure' labels
summary: Chrome's security researchers noticed during field work in India that even tech-savvy people didn't link Chrome's padlock icons with security. A survey of 1,329 Chrome users and tests of 40 icons and 7 labels with thousands of survey respondents led Google to replace Chrome's connection security indicators with 'Secure' and 'Not secure' icons and words, launched in Chrome 53.
problem: Browser security indicators had barely changed since early-2000s research, and Chrome's icons, especially the neutral page icon for plain HTTP, weren't understood. Icons also had to work small, without colour, and for new internet users on phones.
research: Google researchers surveyed 1,329 people in the moment while they browsed, via a Chrome extension (65% outside the US), then evaluated forty candidate icons and seven strings through Google Consumer Surveys, with around 500 respondents per variant.
insight: Most respondents linked the green lock with security, but many had no idea what the plain HTTP icon meant, and many wrongly thought HTTPS guaranteed a site was trustworthy. Shape alone needed to signal risk for colour-blind users, and words were needed to teach meaning.
change: Google selected three indicators: a lock with 'Secure' for HTTPS, and 'Not secure' with neutral and red-triangle icons for HTTP and broken HTTPS. Chrome adopted them in Chrome 53, rolling out 'Not secure' for HTTP gradually to avoid alarming people.
outcome: The paper reports the proposed indicators were adopted by Google Chrome. No post-launch comprehension or behaviour metrics are given.
attribution: Direct. The paper documents the research and states Chrome adopted the indicators it selected.
caveats: Decision only: no measured outcome after launch. Survey respondents were tech-savvy extension users and Google Consumer Surveys panels, and the indicators were not yet tested in countries with many new internet users. Authors are Google employees.

sources.title: Rethinking Connection Security Indicators (Porter Felt et al., SOUPS 2016)

title: Canada's EI maternity and parental benefit pages: task success rose from 28% to 78% in testing
company: Employment and Social Development Canada / Service Canada (with TBS Digital Transformation Office)
summary: Ahead of a new parental sharing benefit in 2019, Canada tested its Employment Insurance maternity and parental benefit pages with 22 working-age people; they completed only 28% of tasks such as working out how long they could take off. A rewritten prototype with a comparison table, worked examples and a simple estimator raised task success to 78% with 20 new participants.
problem: Thousands of parents apply for EI maternity and parental benefits each year, and a new 'use it or lose it' sharing benefit was launching in March 2019. Existing content blurred legally distinct ideas and used jargon, so people couldn't work out their options or amounts.
research: The Digital Transformation Office reviewed other websites and talked with EI service agents, then ran baseline task-performance testing with 22 participants aged 25–39 in full-time work (8 scenarios, 155 task trials). A prototype was validated with 20 new participants (167 tests), with fixes made after observing sessions.
insight: People didn't distinguish 'leave' from 'benefits', didn't realise the choice between standard and extended benefits couldn't be changed later, misread how one parent's choices affect the other's, and confused eligibility weeks with entitlement weeks, latching onto the bigger number.
change: The team reorganised pages to match their headings, hid technical detail in expandable sections, added a table comparing standard and extended benefits, worked examples set out as equations, a simple estimator of benefit amounts and end dates, and a section on special circumstances.
outcome: Overall task completion rose from 28% to 78% and finding the right page from 46% to 90%. Working out maximum leave rose from 5% to 79%; whether a bonus counts in earnings from 0% to 69%. 'Variable best weeks' stayed weak at 53%, and the 80% target was missed, though the 20-point improvement target was met.
attribution: Direct. Same scenarios before and after a redesign built around the baseline findings.
caveats: Prototype testing with small samples (22 and 20) and a narrow participant profile; the prototype was revised during validation. No live-site, call volume or application data reported.

title: Google's data on millions of recoveries showed secret questions fail, so it shifted to SMS and email
summary: Secret questions were long assumed to be a memorable backup for lost passwords. Google analysed hundreds of millions of secret answers and millions of recovery attempts, plus surveys of about 1,500 people, and found answers were both easy to guess and often forgotten. The findings motivated Google to favour SMS and email recovery and keep secret questions only as a last-resort signal.
problem: Many services, Google included, relied on personal knowledge questions ('Favourite food?', 'Father's middle name?') for account recovery, on the assumption that people remember them reliably. Their real-world security and memorability had never been measured at scale.
research: Google researchers studied the distribution of hundreds of millions of secret answers and a month of account recovery claims across languages and countries, and ran Google Consumer Surveys in the US (1,500 respondents for the main survey, plus two follow-up surveys) on why people give untruthful answers and how much they trust each recovery method.
insight: About 40% of English-speaking US users couldn't recall their answers when needed; the questions that were hardest to guess were the hardest to remember. A single guess could crack 19.7% of English speakers' 'Favorite food?' answers. 37% of surveyed people who gave fake answers did so to make them harder to guess, which made answers more predictable, and people trusted secret questions more than SMS, the opposite of reality.
change: Google favoured SMS and email as recovery mechanisms and now uses secret questions only as a last resort, combined with other signals in its login risk analysis.
outcome: Over a full month of recovery claims, SMS recovery succeeded 80.9% of the time, against 60.8% for the best-performing secret question group (down to 44% for French users) and 75% for email. The paper reports the findings 'motivated Google's decision' to favour these alternatives.
attribution: Direct for the decision: the paper states the research motivated the switch. The success rates compare existing mechanisms rather than measuring the effect of the switch itself.
caveats: This is large-scale behavioural analytics plus surveys, not usability testing. No before/after figures for overall recovery success after the change. Authors are Google staff (and a former Google researcher). SMS later became recognised as weaker than other second factors.

sources.title: Secrets, Lies, and Account Recovery: Lessons from the Use of Personal Knowledge Questions at Google (Bonneau, Bursztein, Caron, Jackson, Williamson; WWW 2015)

title: Michigan's benefits form cut from 1,000 questions to 213 after in-home research
company: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (with Civilla)
summary: Michigan's combined application for food, health and other assistance was over 40 pages and about 1,000 questions. Design studio Civilla spent thousands of hours with applicants and caseworkers, then rebuilt the form with them. Early figures showed far more complete applications and much faster case processing.
problem: The state's assistance application was one of the longest in the country: more than 40 pages, roughly 18,000 words and 1,000 questions. Applications came in incomplete and took caseworkers a long time to process.
research: Starting in September 2015, Civilla researchers spent more than 4,000 hours interviewing benefit applicants in their homes and shadowing and interviewing public servants. Clients and staff then tested drafts of the new form.
insight: The form itself was a major source of friction for both residents and staff: much of its length did not help the state decide eligibility, and confusing questions led to incomplete submissions that caseworkers then had to chase.
change: MDHHS replaced the old application with an 18-page, 3,904-word, 213-question version with clearer organization and headings, launched statewide in January 2018.
outcome: Government Technology reported early indications: forms arrived about 94% complete versus about 72% before; case processing time fell 42% (a 10-hour case now took about 5 hours 48 minutes); caseworkers gained about 4 hours 12 minutes per week; paper use dropped 80%; and the state reported no loss of information collected.
attribution: Direct. The new form was designed from the field research and tested with clients and staff; the outcome figures compare the old and new form.
caveats: Early figures reported within weeks of statewide launch, likely from pilot use; no control group and no published methodology for the completeness and timing numbers. Figures come via journalism quoting the state and Civilla.

sources.title: Michigan Scales Back Massive Applications Process with Human-Centric Design

title: Login.gov lifted identity-proofing success from 51% to 74% after user testing
summary: Many people who started Login.gov's higher-assurance identity verification never finished it. The team tested the photo-capture flow with users, found tap-target, wording and screen-order problems, and fixed them. Proofing success rose from 51% to 60% within two weeks and averaged 74% within 30 days.
problem: Login.gov's identity verification flow (IAL2), which asks people to photograph their ID and themselves, had a low success rate: about half of people who started it completed every step.
research: Remote concept testing and user interviews with members of the public, watched by cross-disciplinary team members, with fast iteration between rounds. Participant counts are not given.
insight: Mobile users needed large tap targets and did not reliably hit the small photo button; the word 'selfie' was not universally understood; and an interim verification screen shown after only two steps confused people.
change: Made the whole photo box tappable, replaced 'selfie' with 'Take a photo of yourself', and reworked the unhelpful interim screen, among other plain-language changes.
outcome: Actual proofing success (people who start and complete all steps) rose from 51% to 60% within two weeks of the changes. Within 30 days the average was 74%, with a daily high of 84%.
attribution: Fairly direct: the post lists specific research findings, the changes made in response, and the before/after success rate. It does not rule out other changes or shifts in user mix over the same period.
caveats: Self-reported by GSA on its own platform. No control group, no participant numbers, and the measurement window is short. The rise continued into the 30-day mark, so some of it may reflect other factors.

sources.title: Security Is Everyone's Job: Delivering Secure, Usable Login for Government

title: VA's online health care applications rose from about 62 to 500+ a day after a researched rebuild
company: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (with U.S. Digital Service)
summary: VA's online health care application was a fillable PDF that most browsers couldn't open, so only about 8% of applications came in online. The U.S. Digital Service rebuilt it as a web form on Vets.gov, shaped through research with Veterans. Daily online submissions went from about 62 to more than 500.
problem: The 10-10EZ health care application was a PDF requiring Adobe Acrobat. Only Internet Explorer opened it by default, so about 70% of visitors hit an error. Since 2012 only about 8% of applications had been submitted online.
research: Vets.gov ran usability testing, card sorting and contextual interviews with Veterans, remote and in person, individually and in groups, and worked through bugs and feedback directly with Veterans. The report describes these methods for Vets.gov as a whole rather than for the form alone.
insight: Veterans were blocked by the technology itself (the PDF failing to open) and by having to navigate multiple VA sites with several logins, not by unwillingness to apply online.
change: On June 30, 2016 VA launched a plain HTML health care application on Vets.gov that works in any browser, and kept iterating it based on Veteran feedback.
outcome: Online submissions went from about 62 per day to more than 500 per day; 41,000 online submissions arrived in the first 60 days. In 2015 only about 10% of 582,000 applications were online.
attribution: Partial. The largest gain likely came from replacing a broken PDF, which basic analytics would reveal. The report credits a user-centered process, but the research methods are described for Vets.gov generally, not tied to specific form decisions.
caveats: Self-reported by USDS in its report to Congress. No control group. The improvement mixes fixing a technical failure with research-led design; it is not possible to separate them. Completion rates were not reported.

sources.title: Vets.gov — U.S. Digital Service Report to Congress 2016

title: GetCalFresh cut California's food-aid application from 45 to about 10 minutes
company: Code for America with California Department of Social Services
summary: Code for America watched people try to apply for CalFresh (SNAP) through the existing online system and found it long, desktop-bound and paperwork-heavy. It built GetCalFresh, a mobile-first application with photo uploads and text updates. Application time dropped from 45 minutes to about 10, and the service went statewide in 2019.
problem: Applying for CalFresh online took around 45 minutes, didn't work well on phones, and required faxing, mailing or dropping off documents, so many eligible Californians never applied or never finished.
research: Starting in 2013, Code for America observed applicants navigating the existing enrollment process, ran pilots in counties, gathered insights from county staff and analyzed data on where people dropped off.
insight: The application needed to be much simpler and to work on a mobile phone; document submission was a major barrier; and applicants lost track of what happened after submitting.
change: Built GetCalFresh: a shorter, mobile-friendly application, document upload by phone camera, and text messages confirming submission and reminding people of key steps. Research findings were fed back to county staff to change local processes.
outcome: Code for America and CDSS report that application time fell from 45 minutes to about 10 minutes (under 10 minutes by 2019). The service expanded to all 58 California counties in May 2019. Application rates reportedly rose in counties using it, but no figures are given.
attribution: The product was designed from the observational research, and the time reduction compares it with the old process. The source does not say how the times were measured.
caveats: Self-reported by Code for America, which built and runs the product. The time comparison is between two different systems with no published method. Uptake gains are claimed without numbers.

sources.title: California Launches Code for America's GetCalFresh in All 58 Counties

title: HMCTS online divorce cut error-driven form returns from about 40% to 0.5%
company: HM Courts & Tribunals Service (UK Ministry of Justice)
summary: Research into the divorce process found the paper application form was the biggest source of problems, with around 40% of forms sent back for errors. HMCTS replaced it with a researched, tailored online form and kept refining it from what users got wrong. Error-driven returns fell to 8% in the first online version and 0.5% later.
problem: Under the paper process, up to 40% of divorce applications were rejected or returned because forms were filled in incorrectly, costing applicants time and stress and creating rework for court staff.
research: From April 2016: discovery research with applicants, court staff and support workers (Personal Support Unit, Citizens Advice); end-to-end journey mapping; contextual research; usability and prototype testing, including with front-line staff and at the Digital Accessibility Centre with people with access needs; call-centre and nationwide surveys. A limited pilot at the East Midlands divorce centre began in January 2017.
insight: Of all the documents in the process, the D8 application form caused the most problems. Applicants were making avoidable mistakes about eligibility rules (such as the one-year marriage requirement), jurisdiction and marriage certificate details.
change: The D8 was replaced with an online 'smart form' that adapts its questions to the applicant's circumstances, with in-service guidance and validation against common errors (for example a divorce date before the marriage date). Wording and help were refined after launch, and the paper form was redesigned on the same principles.
outcome: HMCTS reports that about 40% of paper forms were returned for errors; the first online version brought that to 8%, and further work brought it to 0.5% by May 2018.
attribution: Strong link: research identified the form as the problem and the specific errors to design against; the outcome is the error-return rate for that form. Some of the gain comes from validation that any digital form could add.
caveats: Figures are self-reported by HMCTS in a blog post without method detail. Comparing paper to online is not like for like, and early online users were a limited, self-selected pool. An alpha assessment also cited a separate 17% judicial rejection rate, not reported on here.
